articles.title: Italy overturn deficit to beat France 3-1, top Nations League group
articles.summary: Italy rallied from an early goal to defeat France 3-1 at the San Siro, moving level on points but ahead on head‑to‑head, as reported by Al Jazeera.
articles.content:
Italy recovered from a ten‑minute setback to secure a 3-1 victory over France at Milan’s San Siro, a result that placed the Azzurri at the summit of Group A1 in the UEFA Nations League. The win gave Italy ten points, matching France’s tally but granting Italy the top spot because of a superior head‑to‑head record. France’s coach Zinedine Zidane suffered his first defeat in the competition, while Italy’s manager Roberto Mancini extended his side’s unbeaten run to four matches in his second spell in charge.

The opening goal came when France’s midfielder Michael Olise capitalised on a mis‑pass from Italy goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. Olise received the ball directly, evaded a defender and struck home his fifth goal in as many Nations League games – a record only surpassed by England captain Harry Kane’s seven. The strike arrived in pouring rain, underscoring the electric start France produced despite missing their star attackers Kylian Mbappé and Ousmane Dembélé through injury.

Italy’s response arrived in the 26th minute. Nicolo Cambiaghi surged down the left flank, cut the ball back from the byline and set up Francesco Pio Esposito, who finished with a deft touch to level the score. The goal sparked a surge of activity, with Sebastiano Esposito, Francesco’s older brother, forcing a sharp save from French goalkeeper Mike Maignan two minutes later. Bradley Barcola then threatened a third before half‑time, curling a shot that struck the far post.

The second half opened with French winger Rayan Cherki unleashing a rasping strike that Donnarumma tipped onto the post. Italy pressed forward, and Cambiaghi’s drive forced Maignan into a point‑blank save. A penalty opportunity emerged when Cambiaghi was brought down by Malo Gusto, but Sebastiano Esposito’s spot‑kick sailed wide, leaving the score unchanged at the hour mark. Three minutes later, Davide Frattesi restored Italy’s lead, drilling a low shot from a Federico Dimarco cross after Dimarco had been substituted for a fresh attacking option.

The decisive moment arrived when Antonio Vergara, a substitute, was fouled by Dayot Upamecano inside the French penalty area. Francesco Pio Esposito stepped up and sent the ball into the bottom corner, securing a 3-1 lead that would hold until the final whistle. France’s attempts to claw back were thwarted by the woodwork on two occasions, and they also missed a chance when Lucas Da Cunha’s half‑volley drifted narrowly wide. Italy’s goalkeeper Donnarumma made several crucial interventions, including the earlier deflection of Cherki’s effort and a later save that preserved the lead.

The result not only gave Italy three points but also marked their first home victory over France since 1962. By virtue of the head‑to‑head advantage, Italy moved ahead of France in the group, while Belgium, after delivering a fifth straight defeat to Turkiye, sit third with nine points. The final round of group matches will see Belgium host Italy and Turkiye travel to France. Elsewhere in the competition, England secured a place in the last eight after Harry Kane’s penalty win over Croatia, a match that also celebrated his record 126th cap.

Background: The Nations League groups European national teams into mini‑leagues, with each side playing the others home and away. Points are awarded for wins and draws, and the teams with the highest totals advance or avoid relegation, while head‑to‑head results break ties. A penalty is awarded when a foul occurs inside the defending team’s penalty area, giving the fouled side an unimpeded shot from the penalty spot, directly in front of the goal.

The match demonstrated Italy’s resilience and tactical adaptability under Mancini, as the side absorbed early pressure, exploited width through Cambiaghi, and capitalised on set‑piece opportunities. France, despite an early lead and a record‑tying goal from Olise, were unable to recover after conceding the equaliser, and their defensive lapses, including the missed penalty and two strikes against the woodwork, proved costly. The win solidifies Italy’s position as a strong contender in the Nations League and adds a historic chapter to the rivalry between the two nations.

articles.title: Six killed in Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser hospital, health ministry reports
articles.summary: An Israeli air attack on Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis killed six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and injured around 30, prompting accusations of war crimes from Hamas and condemnation from the health ministry.
articles.content:
An overnight Israeli air strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis resulted in six fatalities and roughly thirty injuries, according to the health ministry run by Hamas. The casualties included medical personnel, patients and accompanying relatives. The hospital’s director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, said two missiles struck the building that houses surgical wards and intensive care units, but only one detonated.

The health ministry condemned the incident as a blatant breach of international law, describing it as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions". Among those killed was surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who colleagues remembered as a compassionate and skilled practitioner. Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who survived a head wound, recounted the chaos: "My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told BBC News.

Israeli military officials asserted that the strike was a precise operation aimed at a commander of Hamas’s armed wing and other fighters who, according to Israel, were using the hospital as a command centre. The statement identified the targeted individual as Mohammed Abu Ismail, leader of the Khan Younis Brigade, and claimed that the militants were planning attacks from within the medical facility. Israeli forces said they had issued advance warnings and released an audio recording allegedly sent to a senior Gaza health official, though the hospital’s director denied receiving any such alert.

Hamas rejected the Israeli narrative, labeling it a "blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility". The group accused Israel of spreading false narratives to cover up what it called a new war crime. Local activists also circulated claims that a senior Hamas security figure might have been the intended target, but no independent verification is possible due to the restriction on international journalists in the enclave.

The Nasser Medical Complex, the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serves nearly one million residents. This attack marks the seventh time the facility has been hit since the conflict began. A previous double strike in August 2025 killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers. Video footage posted on social media showed a missile penetrating the five‑storey structure and striking a surgical department, while other clips displayed thick smoke, shattered equipment and scattered beds on the second floor.

Footage captured by a freelance journalist for the BBC revealed extensive damage to an operating theatre, patient wards, a sleeping area for medics, hallways and lifts. Photographs released by news agencies appeared to show an unexploded missile lodged inside the building. Dr al-Fara later told reporters that the al‑Yasin surgery building had been hit by two missiles, with only one exploding, and that the damage to the hospital’s infrastructure was severe.

In the aftermath, medical staff described the difficulty of providing care amid the rubble and darkness. Dr Qdeih explained that he and colleagues had finished work around 00:30 and were preparing to rest when the explosion occurred. He managed to free himself from the debris and described the scene as completely unlit, with no power or lighting.

The strike occurred alongside other violent incidents in Gaza on the same day. Two additional Palestinians were reported killed in separate events: one in an Israeli air strike on a vehicle in Gaza City and another by Israeli gunfire in the Bureij refugee camp. The Israeli military also reported targeting individuals it described as terrorists in Deir al‑Balah and Gaza City.

International humanitarian law grants hospitals a protected status, prohibiting attacks on medical facilities unless they are being used for hostile purposes. The conflict in Gaza has repeatedly seen hospitals struck, raising concerns among human‑rights organisations about potential violations of these protections.

Background: Under the Geneva Conventions, medical establishments and personnel are afforded special safeguards during armed conflict. An attack on a hospital is permissible only if the facility is being used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, and even then, a warning must be given and proportionate measures taken to minimize civilian harm.

Background: The Gaza war began after a large‑scale assault by Hamas on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in significant civilian casualties and hostages. Since then, the conflict has escalated, with daily air strikes, ground operations and a humanitarian crisis marked by widespread displacement, infrastructure damage and limited access to basic services.

The broader toll of the war remains stark. The territory’s health ministry, whose figures are regarded as reliable by the United Nations, reports that more than 1,620 Palestinians have been killed since a U.S.-brokered ceasefire in October, while six Israeli soldiers have died in the same period. Overall, the ministry estimates that over 74,650 Palestinians have lost their lives since the conflict’s outset.

Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate. Recent heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families, compounding the challenges faced by an already strained health system. Access for international media remains limited, as Israel does not permit journalists, including those from the BBC, to enter Gaza, making independent verification of events difficult.

The incident at Nasser Medical Complex underscores the ongoing volatility of the conflict and the precarious situation of health services in Gaza, where hospitals are repeatedly caught in the crossfire between opposing forces.

articles.title: Jaguars Trade Aggressively While Patriots Injuries Threaten Playoff Hopes
articles.summary: The Jaguars bolstered their roster with three deadline trades, while New England’s injury‑laden offense struggles to stay competitive, according to CBS Sports.
articles.content:
At the NFL trade deadline, several teams positioned themselves for a Super Bowl run, but the most notable moves came from the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Chicago Bears, who each added proven talent in exchange for draft capital. Jacksonville’s general manager, James Gladstone, executed three trades on the day before the deadline, the most by any club that season. The centerpiece was a high‑profile acquisition of defensive end Jordan Davis, a deal that required surrendering a first‑round selection, two second‑round selections, and a pair of Day 3 picks. The Jaguars also received safety Bates to replace Eric Murray and added depth on the defensive line, while DaVon Hamilton remains sidelined with a torn quad. These transactions are intended to enhance a defense already ranked second in points allowed and to keep the team competitive now and in the future.

The new pieces slot into a roster that already enjoys a three‑game lead in its division and an offense that ranks fourth in scoring. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence continues to guide a unit that builds large leads early, allowing him to finish games without inflating his passing statistics. Wide receiver Parker Washington has emerged as a playmaker, and running back Bhayshul Tuten has become the primary ball carrier. With the added defensive talent, Jacksonville appears poised to maintain its position atop the AFC and to vie for the conference’s top seed as the schedule eases in the second half of the year.

Looking ahead, the Jaguars face a relatively favorable slate that includes two meetings with the one‑win Tennessee Titans, three contests against teams from the struggling NFC East, and a season‑ending clash with the rebuilding Indianapolis Colts. The only significant test on the calendar is a December 6 matchup against the Chicago Bears, a game that could serve as an early Super Bowl preview.

In contrast, the New England Patriots have been hampered by a cascade of injuries that have eroded the effectiveness of an offense that reached the Super Bowl last season. After a brief resurgence, the Patriots have dropped two of their last three games, the lone victory being a narrow five‑point win over the Miami Dolphins. Their upcoming schedule features five likely playoff teams over the next eight weeks, presenting a steep path back to the postseason.

The injury list is extensive. Running backs Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson are both out, the former dealing with a knee issue and the latter battling a mysterious illness. At wide receiver, Romeo Doubs remains on injured reserve, while A.J. Brown is limited by an ankle sprain and knee concerns. Offensive lineman Alijah Vera‑Tucker also sits on IR, removing a key protector for quarterback Drake Maye. The quarterback’s performance has suffered; in Week 9 he threw three interceptions in a loss to the Green Bay Packers, leaving him tied for the league lead in turnovers.

Because of these setbacks, the Patriots must accelerate the return of healthy players if they hope to secure a playoff berth before the season’s conclusion. The timing of those recoveries will be critical as the team navigates a demanding stretch of games.

The Houston Texans, once winless after four games, have turned their fortunes around with three victories in the next four contests. A season‑high 44 points against the Los Angeles Chargers highlighted quarterback C.J. Stroud’s development, while the addition of wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. and the return of Tank Dell have expanded his receiving options. Despite the offensive resurgence, the defense has struggled to complement the scoring output. Will Anderson Jr. leads the league in sacks and performs at a level worthy of Defensive Player of the Year consideration, yet the unit as a whole has not consistently translated his production into wins.

The AFC South remains out of reach for most teams unless the Jaguars falter dramatically, leaving the Texans in a wild‑card scenario. They sit just 1.5 games behind the division leader, keeping them in contention despite the early‑season deficit.

In the NFC North, the Green Bay Packers are the only club with three losses, making every game crucial as they attempt to climb out of the bottom of a division that often sends all four teams to the postseason. Their upcoming contest against the Minnesota Vikings carries extra significance after a dramatic second‑half comeback by the Vikings in Week 1. With Kirk Cousins at quarterback, the Vikings’ offense is expected to be more potent for the remainder of the season.

The Detroit Lions represent a potential stumbling block for New England. While the Patriots’ offense is depleted, the Lions possess a porous defense that could allow New England to move the ball even without a full complement of starters. The Lions are entrenched in the NFC North battle and require victories each week to remain competitive.

Sunday night’s AFC North showdown between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Cincinnati Bengals will determine sole possession of first place in that division. The Steelers previously won a close 30‑27 game in Pittsburgh, and home‑field advantage could swing the result in the rematch. Quarterback Joe Burrow continues to perform at an MVP level, adding pressure on the Steelers.

Background: In the NFL, the trade deadline marks the final day teams may exchange players for draft picks or other assets. Draft picks represent future selections in the league’s annual draft, where teams acquire new talent from the college ranks. Trading established players for picks allows clubs to rebuild or reinforce specific positions while managing salary‑cap considerations.

Background: Injuries are a common factor that can dramatically alter a team’s trajectory during a season. When key contributors miss time, coaches must adjust game plans, rely on backups, and often alter the offensive or defensive schemes to compensate for lost production.

CBS Sports reported that the Jaguars’ aggressive approach at the deadline signals a commitment to contend immediately, while the Patriots’ injury woes underscore the challenges of maintaining playoff aspirations without a healthy roster.

articles.title: Super League votes to expand to fifteen clubs for 2027 season
articles.summary: BBC Sport reports that Super League shareholders approved adding a 15th team for 2027, opening the door for London Broncos to return.
articles.content:
The governing body of European rugby league announced that its shareholders have given the green light to increase the top‑flight competition from fourteen to fifteen clubs for the 2027 campaign. The decision follows a similar expansion that took place for the 2026 season, when the league grew from twelve to fourteen sides.

Super League represents the highest level of professional rugby league in Europe and is administered by the Rugby Football League. It operates a system of promotion and relegation with the second tier, and its clubs compete for the championship title each year.

The most recent enlargement saw the inclusion of Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique, while Salford Red Devils exited after a financially troubled 2025 season. Those changes brought the total number of clubs to fourteen, a figure the competition has previously held for extended periods, with brief spells of fourteen teams in earlier years.

A league statement confirmed the outcome, saying, "[Super League (Europe)] has passed their decision on to the Rugby Football League board." The statement added, "The RFL Board will now set out criteria and assemble a panel to run the process to judge against it." These remarks indicate that the Rugby Football League will now develop the framework that will determine how the additional slot is allocated.

One club that stands to benefit most from the extra place is the London Broncos. After securing both the Championship Grand Final and the 1895 Cup in the most recent season, the Broncos finished the year at the bottom of the annual grading list, placed behind fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders. Despite that ranking, the club’s on‑field dominance in the second tier has positioned it as a prime candidate for promotion.

The grading system used to evaluate clubs was created by the sport’s strategic partner IMG and draws on data collected over a three‑year cycle. Because the calculation includes the season following the investment by former owner David Hughes, the Broncos received a lower score than Barrow, even though their recent performances have been superior.

Financially, the London Broncos are bolstered by the backing of Australian mining entrepreneur Grant Wechsel and former Australian international Darren Lockyer, who previously starred for the Brisbane Broncos. Their involvement is expected to give the club a stronger fiscal footing than many of its peers, according to forecasts that suggest the Broncos could out‑spend rivals while still managing the loss of central league funding.

The National Rugby League, the governing body for the sport in Australia, has expressed interest in the expansion. Its chairman, Peter V'landys, has indicated that any investment agreement with the NRL would likely require the Broncos to be part of the top flight. While the NRL deal is still being finalised, it is understood that the partnership could be delayed until 2028.

The Rugby Football League will now outline the specific criteria that clubs must meet and will appoint a panel to assess applications against those standards. The exact composition of the panel and the weight given to each criterion have not yet been disclosed, leaving some uncertainty about how the final decision will be reached.

At present, the league has not secured a new title‑sponsorship arrangement, nor has it completed broadcast negotiations or set the fixture list for the 2027 season. These outstanding items add further variables to the planning process and could influence the timing of the final club allocation.

Critics have raised concerns that the grading system may have limited relevance if the RFL board chooses to override its scores in favour of strategic considerations. Some observers argue that the system’s reliance on historical data could be at odds with the immediate performance and financial stability of prospective clubs.

The expansion marks the first occasion the competition will operate with fifteen teams, a milestone that could reshape the league’s structure and commercial landscape. As the RFL moves forward with its assessment process, the London Broncos appear poised to make the leap to the top tier, provided they satisfy the forthcoming criteria and any broader investment arrangements are concluded.

Overall, the approval of the expansion reflects the league’s ambition to grow the sport’s footprint while navigating financial and logistical challenges. The coming months will determine which club ultimately fills the new slot and how the league’s broader commercial agreements evolve ahead of the 2027 season.

articles.title: Spain Considers TikTok Suspension After Child Abuse Probe Finds Thousands of Illegal Videos
articles.summary: An independent study by Maldita.es uncovered over a thousand child sexual abuse videos on TikTok, prompting Spain’s youth ministry to seek explanations and contemplate a platform ban.
articles.content:
Al Jazeera reports that Spanish authorities are weighing the possibility of suspending TikTok after an independent investigation revealed a large volume of child sexual abuse material on the service. The probe, carried out by the nonprofit foundation Maldita.es, focused on the platform during a 35‑day monitoring period in September and October.

The foundation said it identified more than 1,000 videos depicting child sexual abuse, which together had been viewed around 48 million times. In the same period it detected over 20,000 profiles it classified as belonging to suspected paedophiles, including roughly 7,000 accounts based in Spain. The organization compiled a list of about 26,000 accounts it believed were involved in illicit activity and forwarded the information to law‑enforcement agencies.

Maldita.es examined user profiles, comments and live broadcasts, creating its own accounts to test how the recommendation system responded. Within three days, the algorithm suggested 19 livestreams featuring minors, with 15 of those appearing in a single morning, all streamed from school settings. The report highlighted how the platform’s recommendation engine can surface content that puts children at risk.

One documented case involved a livestream by a 10‑year‑old girl in Spain. During the broadcast, an adult male left suggestive remarks, illustrating how minors can be directly exposed to sexualized attention while using the service. The foundation said such interactions are facilitated by TikTok’s gift system, where viewers can send virtual items that cost real money, and the platform retains a portion of those payments.

“Abuse is not hidden away in a little corner and it is not hard to find,” said Clara Jimenez Cruz, co‑founder and chief executive of Maldita.es. She argued that the platform’s design amplifies harmful content rather than containing it.

The Spanish Ministry of Youth and Children has formally requested explanations from TikTok’s parent company, ByteDance, and indicated that a suspension of the service is under consideration. In a post on the social network X, the ministry said it had asked prosecutors to act on the alleged abuse cases and that Minister Sira Rego had called for an urgent meeting with TikTok representatives in Spain.

The investigation broke down the offending accounts into several categories. It identified 231 profiles that posted 1,183 explicit items, 780 accounts that appeared to be used to attract buyers, and more than 10,000 accounts that solicited sexual images in comment sections. When all categories were combined, the foundation reported a total of roughly 26,000 suspect accounts.

“Material you would expect to find only on the dark web is on TikTok,” the report stated, underscoring concerns that the platform’s safeguards are insufficient to prevent the spread of illegal content.

According to the foundation, TikTok removed only about one‑tenth of the material it flagged and blocked roughly a quarter of the illegal posts identified in Spain. The company has faced a series of lawsuits and investigations worldwide over allegations that it fails to protect minors, claims it continues to deny.

The European Union has also warned TikTok that its personalized “For You” feed must be altered to eliminate harmful design features, or the platform could face substantial fines under the bloc’s digital content regulations. This pressure adds to the scrutiny the service is experiencing across multiple jurisdictions.

Background: TikTok’s recommendation engine, often referred to as the “For You” feed, uses a combination of user interactions, video attributes and device information to surface content that is likely to keep users engaged. The system continuously updates its suggestions based on real‑time behavior, meaning that once a type of content gains traction, it can be rapidly amplified to a wider audience.

Background: Online platforms that host user‑generated video and livestream content are required in many jurisdictions to monitor and remove material that depicts sexual exploitation of children. Failure to do so can result in legal liability for the platform and may trigger regulatory actions aimed at protecting vulnerable users.

The Spanish government’s next steps will depend on the outcome of discussions with TikTok and any further evidence presented by law‑enforcement agencies. The situation highlights the growing challenge of policing large‑scale social media services for illegal content while balancing the platform’s role in digital communication.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO under internal probe after alleged spy affair
articles.summary: Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former data‑centre executive accused of Chinese espionage, raising concerns over AI technology security.
articles.content:
Nvidia, the multi‑trillion‑dollar company best known for its AI‑focused chips, announced an internal investigation after its chief executive Jensen Huang was reported to have had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former chief executive of a Singapore‑based data‑centre firm. The relationship is alleged to involve a Chinese intelligence operative, prompting the board to examine whether any proprietary technology may have been improperly accessed.

The alleged affair has drawn attention beyond the personal sphere, intersecting with the broader rivalry between the United States and China over artificial‑intelligence supremacy. US President Donald Trump has previously asserted that "whoever wins AI, wins," underscoring the strategic importance of advanced AI models. Nvidia’s products, described as the best chips for AI workloads, have been in high demand, with a single unit of the latest data‑centre kit priced at £37,000 (about $50,000). Large installations can require hundreds of such units.

In response to concerns about technology transfer, the US administration initially imposed an export ban on Nvidia’s newer devices to limit Chinese access. The restrictions have since been eased, but the possibility that Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed, may have facilitated the movement of Nvidia technology into China remains under scrutiny. Bloomberg reported that Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia equipment in November 2025, a claim the firm denies involved illicit use.

Jensen Huang has publicly advocated for a relaxation of export controls, arguing that a more open approach could benefit both nations. In an interview with the BBC last year, he said, "President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so." His stance contrasts with prevailing sentiment that the AI race is a zero‑sum competition.

The internal review faces several key questions. Investigators must determine whether Alice Huang obtained special access to Nvidia’s latest chips through her relationship with Jensen Huang, and if so, whether any information was passed to Beijing or other parties. While the timeline of the affair is unclear, numerous photographs and videos show the two together at public events, suggesting they spent considerable time in each other's company.

Economic espionage is a long‑standing concern for Western governments, with China frequently accused of conducting large‑scale intelligence operations using both technological tools and embedded agents. If China were to acquire a substantial stock of Nvidia chips, it could potentially reverse‑engineer them to develop domestic alternatives, a scenario that would alarm the Trump administration, which seeks to keep advanced AI capabilities within US control.

Some AI models have already been withheld from the UK‑based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they could be dangerous if widely shared. The United States maintains a policy of restricting early access to its most powerful AI innovations to prevent misuse or competitive advantage.

Beyond the technical aspects, there is concern about any national‑security information that Jensen Huang might have accessed in his role. As a senior figure in the US tech elite, he is described as someone who could meet the President informally and who maintains influential connections. Nvidia has stated that, to date, there is no evidence he transmitted confidential information, and the company’s code of conduct explicitly forbids relationships with clients.

President Trump has expressed personal support for Huang, calling him "honourable" and suggesting there must be a reason for the events that unfolded. The board has also backed the CEO, and despite a dip in Nvidia’s share price, the decline has not been dramatic, indicating that investors have not abandoned confidence in the company’s leadership.

Background: Artificial intelligence models are complex software systems that learn patterns from large data sets, enabling tasks such as language translation, image recognition, and strategic decision‑making. The development of cutting‑edge AI often relies on specialized hardware, particularly graphics processing units (GPUs) that accelerate the massive calculations required. Nations view leadership in AI as a strategic asset, influencing economic growth, military capabilities, and global influence. Export controls are policy tools used to restrict the flow of advanced technology to rival states, aiming to preserve a competitive edge and protect national security.

If Nvidia’s market position were to weaken, the broader AI industry could experience slower progress, given the company’s role in supplying the hardware that powers many research and commercial projects. The firm currently lacks a clear successor to Jensen Huang, who has led Nvidia for more than 30 years and guided its shift toward AI before the trend became mainstream. Colleagues describe him as a demanding leader who expects long hours and high performance, often calling all‑staff meetings to address mistakes and prevent recurrence.

As the investigation proceeds, Jensen Huang has pledged cooperation and expressed a desire to retain his position. The outcome will likely influence not only Nvidia’s internal governance but also the ongoing debate over how closely the United States should guard its AI technologies from foreign acquisition. The situation also highlights the personal vulnerabilities that can intersect with national security concerns, exemplified by the classic "honey trap" tactic.

The case remains open, and further details will emerge as Nvidia’s internal review concludes and any related legal or regulatory actions develop.

articles.title: ANC suffers historic defeat in South Africa local elections
articles.summary: The African National Congress fell to 31% of the vote, losing key metros to the Democratic Alliance and prompting coalition talks, signalling a shift away from one‑party dominance.
articles.content:
South Africa’s ruling African National Congress recorded its poorest performance ever in the recent local elections, a result that underscores a steep decline from the party’s historic dominance since the end of apartheid. The vote, held to elect councillors for the nation’s eight largest cities and hundreds of municipalities, left the ANC with roughly 31 percent of the national share, while its main challenger, the Democratic Alliance, secured about 25 percent.

The drop in support translated into tangible losses on the ground. The ANC was overtaken by the DA in Johannesburg, the economic hub of the country, as well as in the capital city of Pretoria and the sprawling Ekurhuleni municipality to the east of Johannesburg. The DA also retained control of Cape Town, South Africa’s second‑largest city. Despite remaining the single largest party in terms of overall vote share, the ANC’s figure represents a sharp fall from the 46 percent it achieved in the 2021 local vote and well below the two‑decade‑old high of 66 percent recorded in 2006.

Local elections in South Africa determine the composition of municipal councils that manage service delivery, infrastructure and local economic development. When no party obtains an outright majority, as is now common in many cities, parties must negotiate coalitions or power‑sharing agreements within a legally defined period before councils are formally constituted. These arrangements can involve a range of smaller parties and often require compromises on policy priorities.

ANC Secretary‑General Fikile Mbalula described the outcome as “catastrophic”, reflecting the party’s sense of urgency to address the electorate’s discontent. President Cyril Ramaphosa, who also leads the ANC, urged political actors to approach forthcoming coalition negotiations with humility, stating, "Our people’s interest must not be drowned by the quest of political parties or representatives to settle political scores or petty squabbles." The president’s remarks highlighted concerns that partisan battles could eclipse the delivery of essential services.

Political scientists linked the vote to a broader erosion of the ANC’s liberation legacy. Sandile Mnguni, a lecturer at the University of KwaZulu‑Natal, told Al Jazeera that the decline should serve as a warning that the party can no longer rely on its historical credentials to win voter confidence. He warned that unaddressed grievances could lead to even steeper electoral setbacks.

Commentators also pointed to the impact of corruption scandals on the party’s fortunes. Ralph Mathekga, a South African author and political commentator, said the election sent a “strong message” that the public could no longer tolerate the combination of service‑delivery failures and corruption. He noted that voters now view the ANC as the primary culprit rather than a solution to the country’s challenges.

Sipho Seepe, a political analyst and columnist, framed the result as a personal rebuke of President Ramaphosa, whose attempts to project a business‑oriented leadership style have been repeatedly questioned. Seepe argued that the electorate’s verdict signals a shift toward political plurality, with coalitions likely to become the new norm in South African governance.

The Democratic Alliance, seeking to shed its historical image as a “white party”, emphasized its willingness to form coalitions only with parties that share a commitment to clean governance, service delivery, the rule of law and non‑racialism. The DA’s stance reflects a strategic calculation to avoid partnering with the ANC, whose record on basic services such as water, electricity, road maintenance and waste collection was heavily criticized by voters.

The local election outcome reverberates beyond municipal boundaries. In 2024, the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in a national election, ushering in a coalition government and ending three decades of uninterrupted rule. Analysts suggest that the current municipal results reinforce the trend toward a more fragmented political landscape, where no single party can dominate without forming alliances.

The transition to coalition politics carries both opportunities and risks. Proponents argue that the need to collaborate could pressure parties to prioritize performance and accountability over partisan dominance. Critics caution that fragmented alliances may lead to legislative gridlock, delayed decision‑making and instability in municipal administrations.

Nevertheless, scholars such as Mnguni view the evolving situation as a chance for South Africa’s democratic development, provided that political actors demonstrate maturity and place governance above narrow interests. While the prospect of unstable alliances is real, the shift away from one‑party rule may ultimately foster a more responsive and inclusive political system.

The ANC’s internal dynamics are also poised for change. President Ramaphosa is expected to step aside as party leader ahead of the 2027 leadership contest and the subsequent general election slated for 2029. The upcoming leadership battle will likely be shaped by the party’s performance in local governments and its ability to rebuild trust with a disillusioned electorate.

Overall, the local election results mark a pivotal moment in South African politics. The ANC’s historic loss of dominance at the municipal level, combined with the rise of coalition governance, suggests a reconfiguration of power that could redefine how public services are delivered and how political accountability is enforced across the nation.

articles.title: Nvidia launches probe after CEO linked to alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia has started an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, while the board says no security breach is evident.
articles.content:
Nvidia disclosed that it has commissioned an independent inquiry after media reports suggested its chief executive, Jensen Huang, was involved with a person identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy. The company’s board stated it sees no indication that corporate secrets or national security have been compromised and affirmed Huang’s intention to remain at the helm.

In a personal statement, Huang acknowledged that he had been "unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," and said he accepted full responsibility for his conduct, noting that he had fallen short of duties owed to Nvidia’s employees, board and shareholders.

U.S. intelligence agencies have been monitoring a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, who is described in a New York Times report as having close ties to Jensen Huang and being suspected of acting on Beijing’s behalf. Surveillance reportedly captured communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, later identified through a process called "unmasking" as Jensen Huang. The Chinese foreign ministry has rejected the allegations, labeling them as groundless speculation intended to malign China.

The board’s statement said the investigation was launched "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort" and emphasized that protecting U.S. national and economic security is paramount for Nvidia and its shareholders. While the board maintains that it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, it pledged to review all available information.

Former President Donald Trump said he had not spoken with Huang since the investigation became public. He described Huang as a "fine person" but added that one can never be certain about such matters, and he praised Huang’s past contributions to the country. Trump also noted that he had been briefed last year on intelligence suggesting Alice Huang was spying for China, and when asked whether he wished he had acted on that intelligence, he replied that he did not think so, calling Huang an honourable individual.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on the matter, citing the sensitive nature of the issue and the fact that it involved an internal corporate investigation. Reports indicate that Rubio oversaw the drafting of a memo in the previous spring that warned the Trump administration about Huang’s relationship with the Chinese businesswoman.

Congressional leaders have also taken notice. Three Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting his appearance before the committees later in the month to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign espionage. The letter highlighted concerns that the People’s Republic of China might gain access to sensitive U.S. technology and information, noting that such infiltration is a core focus of the committees’ investigative work.

Nvidia remains a pivotal supplier of hardware for artificial‑intelligence development, providing chips to major model developers such as OpenAI and Meta. Its H200 processor, once subject to export restrictions due to fears it could advantage Chinese technology firms, was later permitted for limited sales under conditions set by the administration. The company’s market valuation is reported at roughly $4.5 trillion, and it recently posted record earnings of $215 billion.

Background: AI‑focused microprocessors are specialized silicon designed to accelerate the massive calculations required for machine‑learning models. Because these chips enable rapid training and inference of advanced algorithms, they are considered strategic assets in the competition between the United States and China. "Unmasking" refers to a classified intelligence method in which the identity of a U.S. person who was previously anonymized in surveillance data is revealed to authorized officials for further analysis.

The investigation is ongoing, with both the board and Jensen Huang pledging full cooperation. At present, no evidence has been publicly disclosed indicating that Nvidia’s proprietary technology or national‑security interests have been compromised, but the situation continues to be monitored by U.S. officials and congressional committees. This development was reported by BBC News.

articles.title: Georgia Reclaims Top Spot as Ohio State Drops to 21 in AP Poll
articles.summary: Georgia moved back to No. 1 in the AP Top 25 after a 42‑7 win over Ole Miss, while preseason favorite Ohio State fell to No. 21 following a loss to Oregon, reshaping the college‑football landscape.
articles.content:
CBS Sports reported that "Georgia returned to No. 1 in the AP Top 25 poll on Sunday after dismantling Ole Miss 42-7 in Week 10," putting the Bulldogs back at the summit of the weekly rankings. The victory, a dominant road performance against a solid SEC opponent, lifted Georgia to an 8-1 overall record and a 6-1 mark in conference play, positioning the team as the betting favorite for the national championship.

The shift at the top of the poll was amplified by Miami’s defeat at the hands of Notre Dame, which dropped the Hurricanes to No. 5 after their first loss of the season. Utah and Notre Dame also climbed after convincing wins, with Utah moving up to No. 2 and Notre Dame holding the No. 3 spot. The combined results created a clear pathway for Georgia to reclaim the No. 1 ranking.

The Associated Press Top 25 poll is a weekly ranking of the nation’s leading college football programs, compiled from the votes of sports journalists across the country. Voters assess teams based on win‑loss records, strength of schedule, and overall performance, producing a consensus view of the sport’s hierarchy. The poll influences public perception and can affect postseason considerations.

The College Football Playoff (CFP) determines the national champion through a selection process that evaluates the top teams at the end of the regular season. A committee reviews factors such as record, quality of wins, and head‑to‑head results to choose the four teams that will compete in the postseason tournament. Placement in the AP Top 25 often correlates with a team’s chances of earning a CFP berth.

Ole Miss fell sharply from No. 12 to No. 19 after the 42-7 loss, reflecting the impact of a lopsided defeat on a preseason top‑10 team’s standing. Preseason No. 1 Ohio State also slipped dramatically, as CBS Sports noted "Preseason No. 1 Ohio State fell from No. 11 to No. 21 after suffering a 41-28 home loss to Oregon." This drop marks the first occurrence since 1950 where both preseason top‑two teams have each lost three of their first nine games.

Oregon’s surge from being unranked to No. 18 followed its road victory over the Buckeyes, but both the Ducks and Ohio State sit at 6-3, placing them on the periphery of the CFP conversation as Week 11 begins. Their records illustrate the competitive balance in the latter part of the season, where a single win or loss can dramatically alter playoff prospects.

Utah advanced to No. 2, the highest position for the Utes since 2008, after a 28-20 triumph over rival BYU in a highly anticipated Week 10 showdown. The win, described as the most substantive of Utah’s season, reinforced the team’s status as one of the only unbeaten programs remaining and kept its CFP aspirations alive. BYU dropped five spots to No. 12 following its second loss.

The SEC’s representation in the poll contracted from ten to eight teams after Missouri and Florida fell out following defeats. Missouri, previously No. 19, moved to the “others receiving votes” category after a 34-20 loss to Texas, while Florida, which had been No. 25, failed to receive any votes after consecutive home losses exceeding fourteen points—a first since 1946. The Gators’ 23-7 loss to Oklahoma contributed to their decline.

Replacing the departed SEC teams were No. 18 Oregon and No. 25 SMU, which entered the poll based on recent performances. The shifting composition of the Top 25 underscores the volatility of the rankings as teams vie for limited playoff spots.

The last time Ohio State fell as low as No. 21 was early in the 2014 season, after a home loss to unranked Virginia Tech that sent the Buckeyes from No. 8 to No. 22. The program eventually reclaimed a top‑10 position and captured a national championship under Urban Meyer. This season, however, the path to a CFP berth appears considerably more challenging for the Buckeyes.

Looking ahead, Georgia’s position as the favorite to win the national title is reinforced by its strong record and recent performance against a quality SEC opponent. The Bulldogs’ ability to maintain the No. 1 ranking will depend on continued success against remaining conference rivals and the outcomes of other contenders.

Overall, the latest AP Top 25 poll reflects a reshaped landscape in college football, with traditional powerhouses experiencing setbacks and emerging programs gaining ground. As the regular season approaches its final stretch, the rankings will continue to influence the narrative surrounding the race for the College Football Playoff.

articles.title: UK Government Considers Extending Under‑16 Social Media Ban to Vinted and eBay
articles.summary: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government is seriously reviewing a ban on under‑16s accessing Vinted and eBay as part of a wider social‑media restriction set to start next March, according to BBC News.
articles.content:
The UK government is weighing the inclusion of two popular online‑resale platforms, Vinted and eBay, in the upcoming ban that will prevent children under 16 from using certain digital services. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the BBC that officials are "looking seriously" at adding the sites to the list of restricted platforms in order to protect young users.

The ban, announced by the government in June, is scheduled to take effect in March of the following year. It will initially cover ten of the largest social‑media services, including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and the main YouTube app, while a child‑friendly version, YouTube Kids, will remain accessible. The policy targets services whose primary purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post content, especially those with livestreaming or direct‑messaging features that could expose minors to unwanted contact.

Ebay responded to the speculation by issuing a statement that it looks forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". The company emphasised its focus on providing a trusted marketplace for its millions of customers. Vinted, which reports that its UK user base has reached 17 million, did not reply to requests for comment.

Both platforms already restrict membership to adults. eBay’s terms require all members to be at least 18 because listings involve entering into a contract, while Vinted also states that users must be 18 or older to buy or sell items. The proposed extension of the ban would therefore align the age requirement for platform access with existing internal policies.

The suggestion that Vinted and eBay could be added to the ban emerged after the Sunday Times reported that the government was expanding its scope to include sites popular for second‑hand sales. The newspaper linked the move to concerns that messaging functions on these platforms can be misused by strangers to groom children. It also mentioned that other resale services such as Depop and Facebook Marketplace might face similar restrictions.

Background: Online marketplaces enable individuals and businesses to list goods for sale directly to other users, often facilitating peer‑to‑peer transactions without a physical storefront. These sites typically provide communication tools that allow buyers and sellers to negotiate details, arrange delivery, and resolve issues. While such features support commerce, they can also create opportunities for inappropriate contact if not properly monitored.

Background: A social‑media ban for minors aims to limit exposure to content and interactions that could be harmful, including cyber‑bullying, extremist material, and grooming. Enforcement usually relies on age verification mechanisms, platform compliance, and regulatory oversight. In the UK, the communications regulator Ofcom has recently issued recommendations on how to identify users over the age threshold more effectively.

The broader ban follows a similar measure introduced in Australia last year, where authorities also sought to curb under‑16 access to major platforms. Australian experience showed that many children found ways to bypass restrictions, prompting the UK to adopt a tougher stance. Officials have indicated that the legislation will not only block access but also target specific functionalities, such as chat features on gaming sites like Roblox, which will remain available but with limited communication options.

The government has yet to publish a definitive list of all platforms that will fall under the new rules. However, it has clarified that any service whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which permits users to post material will be considered. This definition could capture a wide range of digital environments beyond the initially named social networks.

Industry reaction has been measured. eBay’s spokesperson reiterated the company's commitment to a safe marketplace while awaiting further details of the proposed legislation. Vinted’s silence leaves its position unclear, though its existing age policy suggests alignment with the intended restrictions.

The upcoming ban reflects growing policy focus on safeguarding children online, balancing the benefits of digital connectivity with the risks associated with unsupervised interaction. As the March deadline approaches, both regulators and platform operators are expected to engage closely to shape the final scope of the measures.

articles.title: AIPAC‑Backed Candidates See Mixed Outcomes in 2024 U.S. Midterms
articles.summary: Pro‑Israel groups funded hundreds of races, winning many contests but losing two‑thirds of the money spent as candidates increasingly distance themselves from AIPAC.
articles.content:
AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, poured tens of millions of dollars into the 2024 midterm elections, supporting candidates in both primaries and general contests. While the lobbying group and its affiliated super PAC, the United Democracy Project, managed to back a substantial number of winners, a majority of the money it spent went to candidates who were defeated.

One of the most visible examples of a candidate rejecting AIPAC money came from Texas state representative James Talarico. During a viral podcast clip he declared, "I’ve never taken money from AIPAC, and I’m not taking money from AIPAC in this campaign," adding that the conflict in Gaza deeply troubled him as a teacher, a Christian and a human being. Talarico won his Senate seat by more than 12 percentage points on November 3, while his opponent, Ken Paxton, received roughly $6,000 from pro‑Israel groups linked to AIPAC.

According to tracking by the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, AIPAC, UDP and related PACs spent about $84 million in the election cycle, with roughly $55 million—nearly two‑thirds—going to candidates who lost. Track AIPAC reported that 234 candidates it backed secured victories, a figure that underscores the group’s continued ability to influence outcomes despite the high rate of financial loss.

In the Senate, AIPAC‑aligned groups were active in at least 32 of the 35 races, spending more than $100,000 on candidates in 26 contests. Of those, 21 candidates emerged victorious on November 3. The organization highlighted its support for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as evidence of its focus on the most powerful Democrats.

The midterms also produced several high‑profile defeats for AIPAC‑backed candidates. In Michigan, the group and its PACs allocated about $30 million to Democrat Haley Stevens in the Senate primary, then added another $9 million for Republican Mike Rogers, both of whom lost to Abdul El‑Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel. In Maine, more than $4.8 million was directed to incumbent Senator Susan Collins, who was unseated by Democrat Troy Jackson. In California, UDP and other pro‑Israel entities contributed over $6 million to Melissa Hernandez in a House race, but she was defeated by Aisha Wahab, a left‑leaning Afghan American who has frequently criticized Israel.

Conversely, AIPAC‑linked spending helped secure wins in several Democratic strongholds. In Missouri, roughly $3 million supported Representative Wesley Bell, who captured an 81‑percent majority in the general election after defeating former Representative Cori Bush in a primary. Earlier, AIPAC‑related groups had funneled $8 million to defeat Bush in 2024. In New York, the group spent about $14 million to aid George Latimer’s re‑election after he ousted a left‑wing Israel critic. A similar pattern appeared in a Maryland primary where UDP contributed more than $4 million to Sarah Elfreth, who later won the general election.

Background: AIPAC operates as a lobbying organization that seeks to influence U.S. policy toward Israel. It does not make direct contributions to candidates after a recent rule change, instead channeling money through affiliated political action committees, including super PACs such as the United Democracy Project. Super PACs can raise and spend unlimited sums but must operate independently of the candidates they support, which can make the flow of money harder to trace.

Rina Shah, a geopolitical adviser and former senior GOP congressional aide, told Al Jazeera, "A few years ago, taking AIPAC support was a no‑brainer for most GOP candidates." She noted that a younger, more America‑First wing of the party is now questioning foreign entanglements, and that the war in Gaza is influencing voter attitudes across the political spectrum.

J Street, another pro‑Israel organization that positions itself as pro‑peace, reported on November 4 that it backed more than 200 candidates with over $13 million, targeting many of the same races where AIPAC was active. The group emphasized its focus on Democrats who adopt a more moderate stance on Israel, and a poll it commissioned indicated that a large majority of American Jewish voters continued to support the Democratic Party in the midterms.

The mixed record of AIPAC‑backed candidates reflects a broader shift in American politics. While the lobbying group still enjoys a strong record of winning seats, the proportion of money lost suggests that candidates are increasingly wary of being associated with the organization. This trend appears across party lines, with both Republicans and Democrats weighing the electoral risks of accepting pro‑Israel funding in a climate shaped by the conflict in Gaza and evolving voter priorities.

articles.title: US Midterms Trigger Sharp Drop in AI-Focused Stocks
articles.summary: Investors pulled back from AI-related equities after Democrats secured Congress, fearing regulatory limits on data centres and AI growth, according to BBC News.
articles.content:
The recent United States midterm elections have sent shockwaves through global equity markets, with the most pronounced decline occurring on the Nasdaq, where many of the world’s largest technology firms are listed. The sell‑off followed the Democrats’ sweeping victories that gave them control of both chambers of Congress, raising concerns that new legislative priorities could curb the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Democratic candidates have highlighted opposition to the unchecked growth of data centres, which are essential for powering AI models. Critics argue that these facilities consume large amounts of water and electricity, potentially raising household utility costs and creating noise, land‑use, and other community disruptions. A Gallup poll released in May indicated that a substantial majority of Americans would resist the construction of a data centre in their neighbourhood, a sentiment that appears to have resonated with voters.

James Talarico, a newly elected senator from Texas, reflected this tension, stating, "While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn." He added that clear, consistent regulations are needed to safeguard Americans while fostering innovation.

The political shift is expected to translate into more vigorous challenges to the current administration’s technology agenda. Texas Governor‑elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, campaigned on a promise to pause new data‑centre construction, positioning herself against tech billionaire Elon Musk, whose companies have recently expanded operations in the state after significant Republican‑aligned campaign spending.

Investors have been reacting to these developments by reassessing the valuation of firms tied to AI hardware, cloud services, and related infrastructure. Tudor Brown, co‑founder of the British chip designer Arm Holdings, explained that market prices are driven by expectations of future earnings rather than present performance. He warned that if anticipated returns diminish, shareholders are likely to divest, noting, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings".

The AI boom, sparked by the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, attracted massive capital into companies that produce processors, networking equipment, and the data‑centre capacity needed to train large models. Research from Goldman Sachs projects AI‑related investment to reach a trillion dollars by 2026, underscoring the sector’s scale. However, the surge in funding has also pushed borrowing costs higher for other industries, creating broader financial pressures.

Public discourse has increasingly featured warnings from AI researchers about the technology’s safety, with some suggesting it could pose an existential risk. These statements have amplified speculation about possible regulatory crackdowns, adding to investor unease.

Background: Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as language understanding, image recognition, and decision‑making. Data centres are large facilities that house servers and networking equipment, providing the computational power and storage needed for AI workloads. Their operation consumes significant electricity and cooling resources, which can impact local utilities and the environment.

Background: In financial markets, stock prices often reflect investors’ expectations about a company’s future profitability. When expectations shift—due to policy changes, technological hurdles, or broader economic factors—prices can adjust rapidly, leading to sharp market movements.

Analysts such as Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights suggest that the political realignment may prompt scrutiny of data‑centre construction, energy usage, and AI deployment. She anticipates that the recovery of tech stocks will be gradual, with investors favouring companies that demonstrate solid balance sheets over those whose valuations are primarily driven by speculative growth.

Brown believes the recent decline may simply be a correction of overly optimistic forecasts that imagined "almost infinite AI growth". He expects a floor to be established, after which the sector will continue to generate revenue, albeit at more modest levels than previously projected.

The market turbulence over the past day appears directly linked to the election outcome, yet concerns about overvaluation pre‑date the vote. Whether the current pull‑back represents a healthy pruning of excess optimism or the early stages of a broader bubble burst remains uncertain. What is clear is that the intersection of politics, regulation, and investor sentiment will shape the trajectory of AI‑related equities in the months ahead.

articles.sourceTitle: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff

articles.title: Oil Traders Divert Russian Diesel Shipments After US‑Russia Deal
articles.summary: Several tankers bound for the United States have altered course, raising doubts about President Trump’s agreement with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel, while sanctions concerns linger.
articles.content:
Al Jazeera reports that three of the four tankers loaded with Russian diesel after President Donald Trump’s October arrangement with Vladimir Putin have changed their intended routes, leaving the United States without any of the promised fuel. The deal, announced shortly after a phone call between the two leaders, pledged more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel for immediate delivery to U.S. and global markets, followed by additional volumes in the weeks that followed. Despite the temporary exemption granted by the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, none of the cargoes have arrived on the U.S. Atlantic coast.

The first vessel, the Talisman, and the second, the Leruo, departed the Baltic port of Primorsk with the U.S. East Coast listed as their destination. Tracking data from marine‑analytics firm Kpler and the vessel‑monitoring platform MarineTraffic showed that, as of Thursday, one tanker was rerouted toward Brazil while the other headed into the Mediterranean Sea. A third ship, still positioned in the North Atlantic, altered its destination from New York after receiving new orders, leaving its unloading point uncertain. The Financial Times also noted that the tanker Beast, which had been sanctioned and loaded at Primorsk in late October, was sailing toward the United States and was currently signaling an Atlantic route.

Long‑range product tankers such as these can transport up to about 100,000 tonnes of diesel per voyage, meaning each shipment represents a fraction of the total volumes discussed in the agreement. The plan called for an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and a further million tonnes shortly thereafter, according to statements made by President Trump on his Truth Social platform. The arrangement permits the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian diesel until early April, effectively reversing the ban on Russian energy imports that the United States imposed after Moscow’s full‑scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Analysts caution that the limited amount of diesel that has actually been dispatched is unlikely to ease the sharp rise in U.S. fuel prices, which have hovered near $6 per gallon for retail diesel, roughly double pre‑war levels. Aarathi Krishnan, chief executive of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera that the first tanker’s cargo equates to “roughly two hours of US distillate consumption” and would have “very little difference to national supply” even if it arrived as scheduled.

The broader context involves a complex regulatory environment. While the Treasury’s temporary exemption allows the sale of Russian diesel that would normally be prohibited, Congress has maintained its ban on Russian energy imports, creating uncertainty for market participants. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill sent a letter to port and terminal operators in her state urging them to reject any ships carrying the fuel, warning that attempts to profit from what she described as illegal trade could result in severe penalties. Lawmakers have also cautioned banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that handling the imports could expose them to civil or criminal liability and trigger future congressional investigations.

Background: Diesel is a middle‑distillate fuel derived from crude oil and refined in large complexes. It is used in transportation, industry and power generation, and its market is closely linked to global oil production, refining capacity and geopolitical events. Sanctions regimes can restrict the ability of sanctioned producers to sell their products abroad, often requiring special licenses or exemptions for transactions to proceed legally.

The hesitation among traders appears rooted in the risk of violating sanctions or facing legal challenges. Matt Smith, an analyst at Kpler, explained to the Associated Press that regulatory and sanctions concerns are likely to keep the cargoes from being discharged on the U.S. Atlantic coast, noting that “it’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov asserted that all the diesel would eventually find buyers, while Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev dismissed reports of the diversions as false, claiming that tankers destined for the United States continue on course.

The situation underscores the tension between the executive branch’s attempt to secure additional fuel supplies and the legislative branch’s insistence on maintaining a hard line against Russian energy. The temporary exemption remains the only legal pathway for the shipments, but without clear guidance on pricing, payment terms or the identities of the companies involved, many market participants are opting to reroute the vessels to destinations perceived as less risky. As the diverted tankers head toward Brazil, the Mediterranean and possibly other ports, the United States continues to rely on existing domestic and allied supplies to meet its diesel demand, while the broader debate over the legality and efficacy of the Trump‑Putin diesel deal persists.

articles.title: Global equities tumble as AI concerns follow US midterm win
articles.summary: European and Asian markets slumped after US Democrats secured a decisive midterm victory, triggering a tech sell‑off linked to AI investment worries, while US indexes showed modest recovery.
articles.content:
The Guardian reported that a sharp decline in European and Asian equity markets on Friday was sparked by the Democrats’ clear victory in the US midterm elections, which had already provoked a steep sell‑off in US technology shares the previous day. The negative sentiment spread from Wall Street to Asian exchanges and then reached London, where the FTSE 100 briefly headed toward its worst single‑day performance since early spring.

In London, the FTSE 100 fell as much as 2.35 percent during the morning session, before ending the day about one percent lower after a late rally in US equities. Germany’s DAX slipped around two percent, France’s CAC 40 dropped close to one percent and Spain’s IBEX eased by a little over half a percent. In the Far East, Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi each lost more than six percent, underscoring the breadth of the sell‑off.

Chief investment strategist Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club described the situation, saying, "The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe." She added that concerns over the slowdown in datacentre construction could undermine the spending surge that has driven recent growth, at a time when investors are already jittery about returns on large‑scale AI projects.

The US market showed some relief on Friday. The S&P 500 rose modestly and the Nasdaq, which had suffered its steepest decline in 19 months the day before, closed up a full percentage point, recouping part of the earlier losses. This rebound coincided with a stronger‑than‑expected jobs report that indicated the economy added a sizable number of positions in October, nudging the unemployment rate lower.

Technology shares were the hardest hit on Thursday, with memory‑chip maker SanDisk plunging dramatically and hard‑drive producer Western Digital also seeing a steep drop. The volatility gauge known as the VIX spiked sharply, reaching levels not seen since the early weeks of the conflict in the Middle East, signalling heightened market anxiety.

Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and the Middle East at CMC Markets, characterised the fallout as "actually a bit of a disaster," noting that clients who were long on indices and stocks faced margin calls and complaints as positions were liquidated amid the turmoil.

Analysts warned that the episode could be only the beginning of further pressure. Chris Beauchamp of IG highlighted that, despite Thursday’s dramatic reversal from Wednesday, lingering AI‑related fears could prompt additional selling. He also mentioned that investors remain watchful for any resurgence of geopolitical tension in the Middle East and for movements in oil prices after a recent dip.

Even with the sharp declines, most major indices remain in positive territory for the year. The Nasdaq Composite continues to sit above the start‑of‑year level, though it remains well below its recent peak. The FTSE 100 has posted a solid gain for the current year, albeit still trailing its record high set earlier in the summer.

Economist Mohit Kumar of Jefferies cautioned against interpreting Thursday’s losses as the start of a broader unwind of AI‑related investment. He argued that AI remains a key growth engine for the US economy and that policymakers are unlikely to abandon the sector, given its job‑creating potential in datacentre and AI infrastructure development.

The sell‑off also touched commodity markets, with copper on the London Metal Exchange poised for its steepest weekly decline since March. Benchmark three‑month copper, a metal essential for semiconductor and automotive manufacturing, slipped further, reflecting the influence of AI‑related sentiment on metal pricing, according to Craig Lang of CRU.

Background: Artificial‑intelligence investment has driven significant capital flows into specialised hardware, software and the construction of large‑scale datacentres that provide the computing power needed for advanced models. The expansion of this infrastructure typically supports related industries, including semiconductor manufacturing and high‑performance computing, and can affect broader economic activity through job creation and supply‑chain demand.

Background: Market volatility indexes, such as the VIX, measure the expected range of price movements in major equity indices. Sharp spikes in these indexes often accompany periods of heightened uncertainty, reflecting investors’ concerns about potential rapid price swings.

articles.title: Evening cravings linked to hormones and habits, experts say
articles.summary: Research shows many people snack after dinner due to hormonal spikes, meal composition and cues, but moderate choices and routine changes can help manage late‑night eating.
articles.content:
A sizable share of adults admit to reaching for food after the evening meal, with surveys indicating roughly one‑third of the population snacking nightly and a particularly high proportion among those in their early twenties. Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu warns that this pattern can raise the probability of weight gain and obesity, especially when eating occurs within two hours of bedtime.

Scientists point to a natural rise in appetite as the day draws to a close. Professor James Betts of the University of Bath explains that the hormone ghrelin, often called the "hunger hormone," tends to be elevated later in the day. He notes, "While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner." This hormonal shift can make it harder to feel satisfied after dinner.

Ghrelin is a peptide produced in the stomach that signals the brain to increase food intake. Its levels typically fall after eating, but the decline is most pronounced after breakfast. As the day progresses, the hormone's influence grows, prompting a stronger desire to eat even when caloric needs have been met.

The nutritional quality of the evening meal also plays a role. Dishes rich in protein, fibre and bulk tend to prolong feelings of fullness, whereas lighter or less balanced meals can lead to a post‑dinner "crash" that triggers snacking. When the body perceives a shortfall in satiety signals, the urge to seek additional calories often emerges.

Beyond physiological drivers, behavioural factors contribute to nighttime nibbling. Some people fear waking up hungry, while others have built routines that associate certain settings—such as watching television—with eating. Over time, these environmental cues can become powerful triggers for cravings.

The brain's reward circuitry further amplifies the pull toward calorie‑dense foods. Dr Beaulieu, who works at universities in Leeds and Moncton, observes that "Our liking and wanting for high‑fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low‑fat foods." This hedonic pull can outweigh signals of fullness, prompting a desire for sweets, salty snacks or rich desserts even after a substantial dinner.

Reward pathways are activated by the taste, texture and energy density of foods, releasing neurotransmitters that generate pleasure. When these pathways are stimulated late in the evening, they can reinforce the habit of reaching for indulgent items, creating a feedback loop that sustains the behavior.

Research on the impact of late‑night snacking on sleep quality remains inconclusive. Some studies link foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars—such as white bread, biscuits and cakes—to disrupted sleep, possibly due to blood‑sugar fluctuations that interfere with hormonal regulation of sleep and appetite. However, distinguishing cause from effect is challenging, as poor sleep itself may increase the likelihood of choosing sugary snacks.

Experts caution that the relationship between evening eating and sleep varies among individuals. While certain foods may affect some people’s rest, others appear less sensitive, suggesting that personal metabolic responses play a significant role.

Practical steps can help those who wish to curb unnecessary snacking. Making dinner more satiating, for example by adding lean protein and high‑fiber vegetables, can reduce the urge to eat later. Planning modest, pre‑portioned snacks and keeping them separate from habitual settings—like the living‑room TV area—may also diminish cue‑driven cravings. Eating without distractions can improve awareness of how much is being consumed.

Dr Beaulieu emphasizes that eliminating evening snacks altogether is unnecessary. Allowing occasional treats in reasonable portions can be more sustainable than strict restriction. Keeping healthier options such as fruit, yoghurt or nuts readily available makes them the default choice, while limiting the presence of highly palatable, energy‑dense items reduces the temptation to overindulge.

Overall, the tendency to snack after dinner appears to stem from a combination of hormonal signals, brain reward mechanisms and learned habits. By adjusting meal composition, managing environmental cues and permitting moderate indulgence, individuals can better align their nighttime eating with health goals.
