articles.title: AI and Tech Stocks Edge Higher After Massive Market Sell‑off
articles.summary: After a sharp sell‑off that erased trillions in value, AI‑linked shares recovered modestly, with the Nasdaq rising 1.1% while Asian markets continued to fall.
articles.content:
Shares of companies tied to artificial intelligence and broader technology have clawed back some ground after a market rout that removed trillions of dollars from valuations. The recovery was led by the Nasdaq Composite, which closed the day up 1.1%, partially offsetting its earlier 5.5% decline. The rebound came as investors weighed mixed signals from the United States, including a surprisingly strong jobs report and political developments that could shape AI policy.

In the United States, the S&P 500 finished the session with a modest gain of 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.4% after hovering near flat for most of the day. The modest rise in the broader market contrasted with the sharper bounce in the tech‑heavy Nasdaq, suggesting that investors were selectively returning to AI‑related equities.

Companies that had seen their market capitalisation shrink by hundreds of billions managed to regain some momentum. Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla were among the names that posted gains, signaling that the worst of the sell‑off may have passed for the most high‑profile AI players.

The recovery was not mirrored in Asian and European exchanges. South Korea’s Kospi fell 6% on the day, with chipmaker SK Hynix dropping more than 10%. Major European indexes in Germany, France and Spain also ended lower, and Britain’s FTSE 100 slipped 1.01%. The downturn in these regions came amid concerns about the impact of the United Kingdom’s recent interest‑rate hike and the prospect of further tightening to curb inflation.

Political factors added another layer of uncertainty. The recent midterm elections in the United States delivered a sweeping Democratic victory, raising expectations that the new Congress will pursue stricter rules for AI and data‑centre development. Democrats have campaigned for new regulations, and their control of both houses of Congress is seen as a signal that AI oversight could intensify.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," said Russ Shaw, founder of Tech London Advocates, in an interview with BBC's Business Today. He added that while he remains a fan of AI, the industry’s communication about its benefits has been lacking. Pierre Baqué, chief executive of Neural Concept, described the recent price swings as a "necessary market correction" and warned that the sector must move beyond unchecked infrastructure spending to demonstrate financial discipline.

Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as pattern recognition, language processing and decision‑making. The Nasdaq Composite is a stock market index that tracks the performance of more than three thousand companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, many of which are involved in technology and growth‑oriented sectors.

The United States also released its latest employment figures, showing that employers added 165,000 jobs in the most recent month, well above analysts' expectations. The unemployment rate eased to 4.1% from 4.2% in the prior month, staying within the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% that has persisted since March. These numbers suggest a resilient labour market despite broader market volatility.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at Premier Miton, noted that while the jobs data may appear secondary to the market turbulence, it underscores that the U.S. economy is operating at a strong pace, potentially reducing the relevance of some market‑focused risk narratives.

Market participants remain cautious about the durability of the rebound. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, described the past week as brutal and highlighted the need to see whether the gains in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq can be sustained after the weekend. He suggested that the coming week will provide clearer signals about the direction of the tech trade.

Overall, the episode illustrates how quickly sentiment can shift in response to political outcomes, macroeconomic data and sector‑specific concerns. While AI‑related stocks have shown signs of recovery, the broader picture remains mixed, with Asian markets still under pressure and investors awaiting further guidance on regulatory developments and economic trends. The reporting draws on BBC News coverage of the market movements and related commentary.

articles.title: Nithya Raman elected mayor of Los Angeles, first Asian‑American to lead city
articles.summary: Nithya Raman, a 45‑year‑old Indian‑born urban planner, won the Los Angeles mayoral race, becoming the city’s first Asian‑American mayor and joining other South Asian leaders of global metropolises.
articles.content:
Nithya Raman, a 45‑year‑old Indian‑born urban planner, announced her victory in Los Angeles on Thursday night, describing the moment as overwhelming. She told supporters that the city had provided her family with immense opportunities, saying, "This city has given me and my family so much," and expressed how moving it was to be elected as an immigrant at this point in American history.

Her win marks a historic milestone for the city, making her the first Asian‑American to hold the mayor’s office. It also places Los Angeles alongside New York and London as major world cities now led by individuals of South Asian descent. Raman identifies as a democratic socialist, adding another progressive voice to the leadership of a major U.S. city after New York and Washington, D.C.

The election took place against a backdrop of a strong Democratic performance in the national midterm contests, where the party secured control of both houses of Congress. The Democratic Socialists of America, which endorsed Raman’s campaign, reported a wave of victories for its endorsed candidates across the country.

Raman’s platform centers on three interlinked challenges: the chronic homelessness crisis, the shortage of affordable housing, and the protection of immigrant communities. She has framed the housing shortage as a moral emergency, arguing that the city’s growing indifference to people living on the streets represents a collective ethical failure. A campaign policy statement warned, "Every time we see one of our neighbors living and dying on the streets, we should be shocked," underscoring the urgency of the issue.

According to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, the city counted roughly 44,000 homeless individuals in 2025, with about 27,000 residing in vehicles, on streets, or in encampments. Raman proposes expanding medical outreach teams for those living in encampments and committing substantial new funding to housing construction. She projects that these measures could cut the number of people sleeping outdoors by half by the time the 2028 Olympic Games arrive in Los Angeles.

Public safety also features prominently in her agenda. Raman has pledged to replace the current police chief, whom she says has lost community confidence after failing to halt federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids. She contended that such raids have created a climate of fear that discourages residents from feeling secure in their own neighborhoods.

While Raman enjoys broad progressive support, she faced tension with the DSA over the inclusion of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel in her platform. Raman has described Israel’s actions in Gaza as "genocide" and advocated for non‑violent protest, legislative measures, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS, as ways for Angelenos to express solidarity with Palestinians. The local DSA chapter ultimately chose to retain its endorsement despite the disagreement.

In her victory address, Raman promised to restore an ambitious, creative, and entrepreneurial spirit to Los Angeles, criticizing the existing status quo as broken and unjust. She emphasized that the city’s future should not be limited by current shortcomings, but rather driven by bold policy reforms.

Background: Democratic socialism combines a commitment to democratic political processes with an emphasis on social ownership and regulation of key economic sectors. Proponents typically advocate for expansive public services, stronger labor rights, and policies aimed at reducing economic inequality. In the United States, the movement has gained visibility through electoral successes at municipal and state levels, often focusing on housing affordability, healthcare access, and climate action.

Raman’s personal journey reflects a blend of academic achievement and grassroots activism. Born in the Indian state of Kerala, she arrived in the United States at six years old. She earned an undergraduate degree from Harvard University and a master’s in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. After a stint back in India working on urban governance reforms in Chennai, she settled in Los Angeles in 2013. There, she co‑founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, a nonprofit that emphasizes the dignity and representation of unhoused residents. She also spent a year directing entertainment initiatives for Time’s Up, an organization created by Hollywood figures to fund legal assistance for victims of sexual harassment.

Raman entered electoral politics in 2019, unseating incumbent councilman David Ryu and becoming the first DSA‑backed candidate to win a seat on the Los Angeles City Council. She credited a robust grassroots organizing effort for that upset. In the mayoral race, she positioned herself as an alternative to the establishment‑backed incumbent, Karen Bass, who had the endorsements of high‑profile Democrats such as Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Raman argued that Los Angeles had reached a "breaking point" and was no longer a place of opportunity for many residents.

Her election adds to a growing list of immigrant‑background leaders heading major global cities. In New York, Zohran Mamdani, of Indian descent, became mayor last year, while Sadiq Khan, the son of Pakistani immigrants, has led London since 2016, and Olivia Chow, who migrated from Hong Kong, has served as Toronto’s mayor since 2023. Raman acknowledges the comparison to Mamdani but stresses her own distinct approach to urban policy.

Al Jazeera reported on Raman’s victory, noting the symbolic significance of an immigrant leading one of America’s largest cities and the potential impact of her progressive agenda on longstanding urban challenges.

articles.title: Share price declines ripple through pensions and jobs
articles.summary: Tech stock sell‑off after US midterms lowers share values, affecting pensions, retirement plans and employment prospects, experts say.
articles.content:
BBC News reported that a wave of selling by investors following the United States mid‑term elections has pushed down the share prices of major technology companies. The decline has been linked to expectations that progress in artificial intelligence may slow, even though the sector had previously enjoyed strong gains.

When a company expands it can issue new shares, which are then bought and sold on exchanges such as the London Stock Exchange. The collective movement of these shares is often summarised by indices like the FTSE 100, although many people do not think about these numbers in everyday conversation. Nonetheless, the performance of the stock market can have tangible effects on personal finances.

A large proportion of the population holds a pension, either through a private arrangement or via their employer. In defined contribution schemes, the money saved is invested in assets that include equities. Because the value of those investments moves with the market, a broad fall in share prices can reduce the size of pension pots. Hundreds of billions of pounds are currently held in such schemes, meaning that sizable market swings can influence the retirement savings of millions.

Pension savers typically rely on professional managers to allocate their contributions. Experts stress that pensions are a long‑term investment and that short‑term market turbulence should not prompt panic or hasty withdrawals. As people near retirement, many shift a portion of their holdings into lower‑risk assets such as government bonds, which can perform better when equities are under pressure. However, retirees who are already drawing an income from their pots will still see their returns fluctuate with market movements, potentially affecting the amount they receive.

"the markets" matter for future pensions, according to financial specialists, because the value of the underlying investments directly shapes the size of the pot that will fund retirement income. When markets decline for an extended period, the impact can also reach the labour market. Investors expect a return on the capital they provide to companies; sustained lower share prices may lead firms to cut costs, including staff reductions, as they seek to restore profitability.

In purely investment terms, a drop in share prices can create buying opportunities for those who hold stocks or stocks‑and‑shares Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs). The recent sell‑off followed a period of strong gains, so many long‑term investors may still be ahead despite the current dip. Financial regulators and advisers continue to warn that investments can rise as well as fall and recommend diversification across different asset classes to spread risk.

Some investors choose tracker funds that aim to mirror the performance of a specific index, such as the FTSE 100. While these funds move in line with the broader market, experts underline the importance of maintaining a cash reserve for unexpected expenses, ensuring that short‑term needs do not force the sale of investments at an inopportune moment.

The UK government is actively encouraging individuals to invest more, arguing that higher participation can support economic growth. A recent advertising campaign featuring a character called Savvy the Squirrel was funded by several large financial‑services firms. The initiative has drawn comparisons with earlier promotional efforts, such as the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s that urged people to invest in newly privatised utilities.

Beyond pensions and employment, fluctuations in equity markets can affect currency values and exchange rates, which in turn influence the price of imported goods and services. Changes in oil prices and other global economic factors also feed into the cost of living, creating a complex web of influences that extend from the stock exchange to household budgets.

Background: A share represents a unit of ownership in a company. When investors buy shares, they provide capital that the company can use for growth, and in return they may receive dividends and benefit from any increase in the share price. Defined contribution pensions differ from defined benefit schemes in that the retirement income depends on the amount contributed and the performance of the invested assets, rather than a predetermined payout.

Background: Investment strategies typically balance risk and reward over time. Diversification spreads exposure across various sectors and asset types, reducing the impact of any single market movement. Long‑term investors often adopt a buy‑and‑hold approach, aiming to benefit from overall economic growth while weathering short‑term volatility.

Overall, the recent decline in technology share prices illustrates how movements in the equity market can cascade through pension values, retirement planning, employment decisions and broader economic conditions. While the immediate effect may be a reduction in the worth of investment‑linked savings, financial advisers recommend maintaining a diversified, long‑term perspective and ensuring that cash reserves are available for unforeseen costs.

articles.title: Rural Voters Turn Away From Republicans Amid Inflation Concerns
articles.summary: A Harris poll for The Guardian found sharp drops in Republican support among rural voters, driven by high fuel costs and a perceived affordability crisis, contributing to the party’s losses in the midterm elections.
articles.content:
A poll commissioned by the Harris Poll for The Guardian revealed a dramatic erosion of support for the Republican Party among voters in rural areas, a group that had previously formed a cornerstone of former President Donald Trump’s electoral base. The survey, conducted in the weeks leading up to the November midterm elections, linked the decline to widespread anger over rising living costs, particularly the price of gasoline and diesel.

Across the nation, an overwhelming majority of respondents – 95% – said they were living through an affordability crisis, a sentiment that was amplified by steep increases in gas and grocery prices. By the time the election approached, 61% of voters believed the country was in a recession, even though official metrics did not confirm a technical recession.

The impact of inflation was felt in a range of occupations that rely heavily on transportation. Loggers in Maine reported that tariffs on Canadian wood products were further weakening an already fragile industry. In Texas, drivers with three‑hour commutes were spending roughly $400 each month on fuel, while Midwestern farmers described how higher diesel costs were compounding the challenges of a drought‑affected growing season.

Republican confidence in the economy also slipped sharply. In February, just before the conflict with Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was improving. By October, that share had fallen to 28%, indicating a loss of optimism among the party’s own voters.

Rural voters were especially likely to say that rising gas prices were damaging their finances and that they were operating in “economic survival mode.” They were also marginally more inclined than urban and suburban voters to view corruption as a bigger problem for Republicans, suggesting a perception that elected officials were using their positions for personal gain.

The poll showed that, in the month before the midterms, the proportion of rural Americans who thought the economy was getting worse rose by 17%, compared with a 5% increase among suburban voters and a 3% rise among urban voters. This widening gap underscored the particular strain felt in less densely populated areas where long‑distance travel is routine.

Amid this backdrop, former President Trump attempted to project a more optimistic narrative. "I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote," he said at a rally near the Lincoln Memorial, adding that he hoped voters would "do the right thing." The contrast between his upbeat remarks and the poll’s depiction of everyday hardship was stark.

When voters went to the polls, the Republican losses in competitive races from Maine to Texas translated into a Democratic majority in Congress for the next two years. The outcome highlighted the electoral cost of the affordability crisis that many voters said had dominated their daily lives.

Democratic leaders pledged to focus on issues that dominated the campaign, including the administration’s immigration policies, perceived corruption in the White House, rising health‑care costs, and the broader economy, with particular attention to high prices.

Republican figures began to assess the role that price pressures played in the defeat. Senator JD Vance remarked that the loss was the "cost to pay" for the war with Iran, emphasizing that any honest discussion about the party’s future must start there.

Even before the midterms, polls indicated uncertainty about which party could resolve the affordability crisis. When asked which party offered a solution, 34% of respondents said neither did, while Democrats edged ahead of Republicans with 27% to 24% respectively.

Background: Inflation describes a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services, which erodes the purchasing power of money. Rural voters typically reside in areas with low population density, often relying on personal vehicles for long commutes to work, school, and essential services.

Background: Economic sentiment surveys measure how individuals perceive the health of the economy, including their personal financial situation and expectations for the future. Such perceptions can influence voting behavior, especially when voters feel that basic necessities are becoming unaffordable.

articles.title: Pharma Companies Test Space‑Based Crystal Growth for Future Cancer Drugs
articles.summary: Varda Space Industries has launched three orbital capsules to grow cancer‑drug crystals in microgravity, marking a step toward commercial space manufacturing, while regulators and other firms watch the emerging market.
articles.content:
A trio of capsule‑sized laboratories, each roughly the size of a washing machine, now circles the planet at an altitude of about 300 miles. Inside one of these free‑flyers, researchers are cultivating minute crystals of a candidate cancer medication, taking advantage of the weightless environment to encourage more orderly crystal formation. The other two capsules are conducting experiments on heat‑shield materials and navigation technologies needed for the capsules’ high‑speed re‑entry through Earth’s atmosphere. The missions, carried out by California‑based Varda Space Industries, represent a tangible move toward a commercial sector that envisions manufacturing drugs and other high‑value materials in space.

Varda launched two of the capsules on 1 October and a third on 20 October, achieving the first instance of three of its spacecraft being simultaneously operational in orbit. The company’s chief executive, Will Bruey, described the achievement as a historic first, saying, “We’re the first company in human history to launch multiple commercial re‑entry vehicles simultaneously, and as the frequency of launches increases, the once ‘crazy future’ of manufacturing products in space is becoming more and more certain.”

The primary attraction of the orbital environment is the near‑absence of gravity. On Earth, gravity causes suspended particles in liquids to settle and creates density‑driven currents, both of which can disrupt crystal growth. Dr Meganne Christian, mission manager for in‑space manufacturing at the Satellite Applications Catapult, explained that eliminating these effects allows crystals to develop in a more ordered fashion, noting, “If you are able to remove those effects, you can make crystals grow in a much more ordered sort of way.”

Background: In a microgravity setting, fluids behave differently because buoyancy‑driven convection is largely suppressed. This stability can lead to larger, more uniform crystals, which are valuable in pharmaceuticals where crystal size and shape influence dissolution rates, stability, and delivery methods. The same principles apply to semiconductor and advanced material production, where fewer defects can improve performance.

For drug developers, the ability to grow crystals with precise characteristics could enable reformulation of medicines that currently require intravenous delivery into more convenient injection formats. Improved crystal quality can also enhance the stability of compounds, potentially extending shelf life and simplifying logistics. While the current experiment focuses on a potential cancer therapy, the broader implication is that space‑based crystal growth might unlock new formulations for a range of treatments.

Beyond pharmaceuticals, other high‑tech sectors stand to benefit. Semiconductor manufacturers, for example, could use the microgravity environment to produce purer crystals with reduced defect rates. Dr Christian expressed interest in applying the same approach to graphene, a material prized for its strength and conductivity but prone to defects when produced on Earth. She suggested that a defect‑free crystal lattice could dramatically improve material performance.

Historically, the International Space Station has served as a platform for microgravity research, but its design was never intended for large‑scale manufacturing, and it is slated for retirement around 2030. The transition to dedicated commercial stations and autonomous laboratory capsules is therefore seen as a necessary evolution for industrial space activities. Companies such as the UK‑based BioOrbit have already sent compact labs to the ISS to explore self‑administered cancer drug production, indicating a growing ecosystem of space‑based pharmaceutical research.

Varda’s approach relies on fully autonomous capsules that hitch rides on commercial launch vehicles, most notably those operated by SpaceX. After completing their experiments, the capsules detach, survive a high‑speed atmospheric plunge, and descend under parachutes to remote, uninhabited areas for recovery. This method removes the need for crewed presence, addressing concerns about human‑induced vibrations and safety that can affect delicate manufacturing processes.

The company plans an aggressive launch schedule, targeting seven additional missions in 2027 and ten more in 2028. Frequent flight opportunities are crucial for drug development timelines, where waiting years between experimental runs would be incompatible with modern expectations. Michael Reilly, Varda’s chief strategy officer, emphasized that rapid iteration is essential to keep pace with the speed of contemporary pharmaceutical pipelines.

Other firms are pursuing parallel strategies. Cardiff‑based Space Forge is developing a hybrid model in which semiconductor crystals grown in orbit serve as seed wafers for larger‑scale Earth‑based production, akin to using a starter culture in baking. Its inaugural spacecraft, ForgeStar‑1, has demonstrated key steps toward creating such seed wafers, though a complete manufacturing cycle and return to Earth have yet to be achieved. Co‑founder and CTO Andrew Bacon noted that industry attention has risen sharply since 2018, suggesting the sector is entering a new industrial phase.

Despite the optimism, significant hurdles remain. Demonstrating that the added cost of space manufacturing translates into tangible value is essential. Dr Christian cautioned that not every application will be economically viable and that the industry must focus on high‑value use cases where microgravity offers a clear advantage. Regulatory frameworks will also need to evolve; the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency is expected to issue guidance later this year on how existing drug regulations apply to products manufactured beyond Earth.

Consistency and repeatability are another critical challenge. For any manufacturing process to become commercially sustainable, it must reliably produce the same quality output across multiple runs. Dr Christian highlighted that the capsules must prove they can deliver consistent results repeatedly before the approach can be deemed viable for large‑scale adoption.

The Guardian reported on these developments, noting that the convergence of falling launch costs, increased launch frequency, and advancing autonomous laboratory technology is driving the sector toward a potential turning point. As more companies demonstrate the feasibility of space‑based production, the prospect of a new market for high‑precision materials and medicines appears increasingly realistic, though its ultimate scale will depend on continued technical success and regulatory accommodation.

articles.title: Hebron’s Rooftop Settlements Threaten Palestinian Identity in Old City
articles.summary: Israeli settlers are erecting prefabricated units atop Palestinian shops in Hebron’s Old City, prompting local merchants to resist amid longstanding restrictions.
articles.content:
Hebron’s Old City, a historic quarter in the occupied West Bank, is witnessing a new wave of settlement activity that places prefabricated structures on the rooftops of Palestinian commercial buildings. The expansion, reported by Al Jazeera, is seen by residents as an attempt to alter the demographic and cultural character of the neighbourhood, which has been home to Palestinian families for generations.

Yusuf al‑Khatib, a 65‑year‑old tailor, inherited his shop from his father, who began working there roughly eight decades ago. Yusuf grew up assisting his father from the age of five and has continued the family trade for nearly six decades. He describes the shop as the cornerstone of his livelihood, saying, "This shop is my livelihood and the livelihood of my family. It enabled me to raise my children and provide them with an education." The shop, located on Shalala Street, now shares its roof with newly installed Israeli settlement units.

On 29 October, settlers placed mobile structures on the rooftops of several commercial buildings in the area, creating space for about twenty additional settlement units. Activists argue that this construction will further erode the Palestinian character of the district. Yusuf’s own shop is directly affected, as the new outpost sits above his workshop. Despite the looming threat, he remains determined to keep the shop operating, viewing it as an inheritance that must be protected.

Other shop owners report similar pressures. Bader al‑Daour al‑Tamimi, a father of four university students, observes that the rooftop above his store has already been turned into a settlement outpost. He worries that continued expansion could eventually force him out of his only source of income. Many merchants now face the daily uncertainty of whether they will be allowed to open their doors, given the constant presence of settlers and the occasional involvement of soldiers.

Adel Mustafa al‑Shuyukhi, a 67‑year‑old vendor who also inherited his business, emphasizes the deep personal and communal ties that bind residents to the Old City. Having spent roughly half a century working in the neighbourhood, he knows each corner and each fellow shopkeeper. For al‑Shuyukhi, keeping his shop open is not merely an economic decision but a statement of cultural continuity. He has told his children that they should continue the family business if anything happens to him, underscoring a collective resolve not to abandon the area.

Settlements in the occupied territories are considered illegal under international law, a status reiterated by numerous United Nations resolutions. In Hebron, the situation is compounded by a unique administrative arrangement known as the Hebron Protocol, which split the city into two zones: H1, where the Palestinian Authority handles civil and security matters, and H2, which remains under Israeli security control and includes the Old City and surrounding settlement neighborhoods. This division has allowed Israeli settlers to live among Palestinian residents while imposing stricter movement and access restrictions on the latter.

The roots of the current tension trace back to the 1994 incident at the Ibrahimi Mosque, when an Israeli settler killed dozens of worshippers. Following the massacre, Shuhada Street was closed to Palestinians, and the once‑bustling market that sold vegetables, poultry, camels and carpentry goods began to shrink. Over the years, additional military gates and checkpoints have limited Palestinian access to commercial areas, further isolating the community.

Recent developments have intensified the sense of encroachment. The Old Municipality building, a symbol of Palestinian municipal authority, was seized and converted into a military position, while Arabic street names have been replaced with Hebrew ones. Israeli flags now fly above settler structures, reinforcing the perception of an ongoing campaign to reshape the city’s identity.

Issa Amro, a 46‑year‑old activist and founder of Youth Against Settlements, places the latest expansion within this broader historical pattern. He notes that settlers previously operated within confined zones, but now they are extending beyond areas that have been closed since 1994, reaching the Old Municipality building and the rooftops of commercial properties. Amro argues that the cumulative effect of these restrictions is to pressure Palestinian residents to leave, thereby expanding the settlement footprint.

Despite the mounting challenges, many shop owners remain steadfast. Their determination to keep their businesses open reflects a broader effort to preserve the Palestinian presence and heritage of Hebron’s Old City. By maintaining daily operations, they aim to counteract attempts to alter the neighbourhood’s demographic composition and to assert their right to remain in the place their ancestors built.

articles.title: CVS Health Announces Plan to Split Into Separate Pharmacy and Insurance Companies
articles.summary: CVS Health said it will divide into two publicly traded firms by early 2028, separating its retail pharmacy network from its insurance and pharmacy‑benefit‑manager operations.
articles.content:
CVS Health disclosed on Wednesday that it intends to break itself into two distinct public companies, with the separation slated for the first half of 2028. The move would create one entity focused on the company’s roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies and another that houses its insurance operations and the Caremark pharmacy‑benefit manager (PBM).

The proposed split would unwind the $78 billion purchase of insurer Aetna and dismantle the vertically integrated structure the company assembled after the 2018 acquisition. A board‑led comprehensive strategic review prompted the decision, according to the company’s release.

The announcement marks a sharp reversal of a two‑decade effort to position CVS as a one‑stop health destination. It also coincides with a turnaround program led by CEO David Joyner, which targets $2 billion in cost reductions, store closures, leadership changes, and tighter control of Medicare Advantage expenses.

Joyner said, "From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination." Since he assumed the role in October 2024, CVS shares have risen about 70 percent, lifting the company’s market value to roughly $117 billion.

Both successor firms will be listed on public exchanges. The insurance and PBM arm will retain the CVS Health name and remain under Joyner’s leadership, while the pharmacy‑only business will be branded CVS Pharmacy and will be headed by Prem Shah, currently group president of CVS Health. Additional executive and board appointments are slated for a later announcement.

Current CVS shareholders will receive proportional stakes in each of the new companies, ensuring continued ownership across the split.

Financially, the pharmacy segment generated $37.66 billion in sales for 2025, the insurance unit posted $36.29 billion in revenue, and the broader health‑services segment contributed $51.24 billion. In the most recent quarter, total sales rose to $108.40 billion from $102.87 billion a year earlier, surpassing Wall Street forecasts. Growth in the health‑care benefits and services divisions drove the increase, even as pharmacy‑services revenue slipped year over year.

The company also said it will combine its insurer and PBM with primary‑care provider Oak Street Health, home‑visit service Signify Health, and its specialty‑drug business, consolidating these operations under the insurance‑focused entity.

According to CVS, the separation will enable each company to pursue a more focused strategic agenda, accelerate innovation, adopt new technologies, and improve operational efficiency.

Background: A corporate split involves a parent firm dividing its assets and operations into two or more independent companies, each with its own management, board, and public listing. The process typically aims to unlock shareholder value by allowing the resulting entities to concentrate on distinct market opportunities and strategic priorities.

Background: Pharmacy‑benefit managers negotiate drug prices and administer prescription benefits for insurers and employers. Critics argue that PBMs can create opacity in pricing, wield significant market power, and face conflicts of interest when owned by entities that also run pharmacies or insurance businesses.

Analyst Michael Cherny of Leerink Partners described the breakup as “a complete shock” but noted that the retail pharmacy operation has been gaining market share and stabilizing gross margins after the introduction of the CostVantage reimbursement model last year. He added, "In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," and suggested that the split may also help the company avoid ongoing state legislative scrutiny of its vertical integration.

Regulatory pressure on PBMs has intensified, with bipartisan scrutiny at the federal level and a wave of state actions aimed at limiting PBM ownership of pharmacies. Recent congressional reforms altered how PBMs are compensated under Medicare Part D, while several states have moved to restrict the practice of PBMs owning retail pharmacy outlets.

The announcement was reported by CNBC, noting that the split would create two publicly traded companies and that existing shareholders will retain stakes in both entities after the separation.

articles.title: Trump moves to cut South Africa and Rwanda from US Trade Deal
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has announced plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act by 1 January 2027, citing security, trade barriers and eligibility concerns, according to BBC News.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump has formally informed Congress that the United States intends to end the participation of South Africa and Rwanda in the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) starting 1 January 2027. The decision follows an annual review by the U.S. Trade Representative’s office, which concluded that both nations were not meeting the programme’s eligibility standards.

AGOA, a preferential trade arrangement, allows qualifying African countries to ship a wide range of products to the United States without tariffs. The scheme is intended to promote economic development and deepen trade ties between the United States and the continent.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the review identified practices in the two countries that conflicted with the programme’s requirements. He added that the administration had already sent formal notifications to the governments of South Africa and Rwanda. Greer also stated, "The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria." 

In a letter addressed to President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump argued that South Africa’s actions on international security and its cooperation with governments viewed unfavourably by Washington posed risks to U.S. national security and foreign policy. The president also accused Pretoria of maintaining substantial obstacles to American trade and investment, citing restrictions on agricultural market access, regulatory hurdles, investment protections and intellectual‑property rules.

South Africa’s Trade Minister Parks Tau called the move "unfortunate" and said that Washington was raising new issues that had not been part of the trade talks that began in 2025. He emphasized that South Africa would continue to broaden its export markets to safeguard jobs.

South Africa has sought to contextualise the potential loss of AGOA benefits, noting that the bulk of its trade with the United States occurs outside the preferential scheme. Government data show that about 89 % of South African exports to the U.S. in 2025 entered under ordinary World Trade Organization most‑favoured‑nation terms, while roughly 10 % benefitted from AGOA, down from 28 % the previous year. The value of exports under the programme fell to about $1.7 billion in 2025, compared with $4 billion in 2024. Bilateral trade reached $28.8 billion in 2025, and more than 600 American companies operate in South Africa, supporting around 134,600 jobs.

Pretoria highlighted the complementary nature of the two economies. South Africa supplies 12 of the 50 minerals the United States deems critical and provides about 70 % of the isotopes used in American cancer treatment. South African manufacturers also rely on U.S. inputs for products such as vehicles and boats that are exported under AGOA.

Oxford Economics senior economist Jee‑A van der Linde warned that the U.S. decision could increase pressure on South Africa’s manufacturing sector, noting that displaced exports may be hard to redirect amid global trade disruptions and competition from low‑cost Chinese imports, especially in the automotive field. He observed that South Africa has previously managed to shift some tariff‑affected goods to markets in Europe and China.

U.S. Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III described the outcome as regrettable, saying South African policies led to the termination from AGOA. He wrote on the social platform X that the result was "predictable and preventable" given the South African government’s rejection of U.S. concerns.

Rwanda faces a similar fate. Washington’s review raised issues related to human‑rights practices, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers’ rights. The move follows a recent U.S. Treasury sanction on Rwanda’s defence ministry for alleged involvement with the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Rwanda denies the allegations despite what the Treasury described as overwhelming evidence.

Rwanda’s exports to the United States rose to $43.3 million in 2025 from $13.1 million in 2024, according to import data. Oxford Economics economist Alexander Venter noted that the United States accounted for about 2 % of Rwanda’s merchandise exports in 2025, with only around 4 % of those exports benefiting from AGOA preferences. He added that neighbouring African nations and Asian markets continue to dominate Rwanda’s trade.

The termination of AGOA benefits for both countries arrives amid already strained diplomatic relations. Last year, President Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and announced a programme offering asylum to white Afrikaners, repeating widely discredited claims of a genocide against the white population. The current trade action adds another layer of tension, potentially limiting the two nations’ access to preferential U.S. market treatment.

Both governments have signalled intent to mitigate the impact. South Africa stresses the broader trade relationship beyond AGOA, while Rwanda points to growing exports to other regions. Analysts suggest that the loss of duty‑free access could compel both economies to seek alternative markets and adjust supply chains, though the transition may be challenging given existing dependencies on U.S. inputs and demand.

The developments underscore the intersection of trade policy with broader geopolitical and security considerations, reflecting Washington’s willingness to leverage economic tools to address concerns it deems critical to national interests.

articles.title: Investigators Probe Possible In‑flight Breakup in Florida Learjet Crash
articles.summary: The NTSB is examining whether a Learjet 60 disintegrated before its fatal descent near Mar‑a‑Lago, with ice, turbulence and structural failure under review, BBC News reports.
articles.content:
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board announced a probe into a fatal Learjet 60 accident that occurred on a Florida roadway less than ten miles from President Donald Trump's Mar‑a‑Lago estate. The board will assess whether components of the aircraft separated before it entered a steep nose‑down plunge that ended in a fiery crater, killing all nine occupants.

The jet had departed Austin, Texas, bound for the Bahamas on a Sunday morning. Shortly after take‑off, the crew reported encountering precipitation and moderate turbulence, requesting a climb to a higher altitude. Within half a minute, the aircraft began an uncontrolled descent, prompting the pilots to issue a mayday call. The subsequent transmission grew unintelligible, and the final recorded words from the cockpit indicated a loss of time to recover.

Air traffic control audio captured a crew member declaring an emergency, shouting, "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute," before adding, "we are going to crash into the ground." About thirty‑five seconds later, the last audible phrase was "we're out of time." These statements illustrate the rapid loss of control experienced by the flight crew.

Investigators are also focusing on environmental factors. The NTSB confirmed that ice and turbulence were present during the flight, and thunderstorms had been reported in the vicinity at the time of the crash. Determining how these conditions may have contributed to the aircraft's behavior will be part of a lengthy investigative process.

The crash site was Military Trail, a six‑lane commercial road lined with businesses and residences. The impact created a large crater, and debris was scattered across nearby sports fields, storefronts and homes. Officials noted that the pattern of wreckage could indicate that the aircraft broke apart before striking the ground, a hypothesis that will be examined through forensic analysis of the recovered pieces.

Among the nine victims were a tech entrepreneur, his wife, their two children, a 20‑year‑old copilot, and several other passengers. The entrepreneur, identified as Adam Robinson, traveled with his wife Helen Sharp and their children Emma and Charlie. The other passengers named by family statements were Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina. The pilot, reported in media outlets as Jeffery Gregory, was accompanied by copilot Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence at the age of 17.

A single ground casualty suffered a leg injury when the aircraft impacted the roadway. Emergency responders worked to extract the injured individual while also securing the crash zone for investigators.

Recovery of the wreckage presents a formidable challenge. Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the board, described the effort to retrieve debris from the crater as "daunting." The investigation team includes representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, meteorologists and air‑traffic control experts, all collaborating to piece together the sequence of events.

One technical question under review is whether a cockpit voice recorder was installed on the Learjet and, if so, whether it can be recovered. The presence of such a device could provide critical insight into the crew’s actions and the aircraft’s performance in the moments before impact.

Background: The NTSB is an independent federal agency tasked with investigating accidents across all modes of transportation, issuing safety recommendations to prevent future incidents. The Learjet 60 is a midsize business jet commonly used for private and corporate travel, known for its speed and range capabilities.

The investigation will involve detailed flight‑data analysis, examination of recovered components, and review of weather reports. Flight analysis has already shown that the jet was descending at a rate of hundreds of feet per second before impact, underscoring the severity of the loss of control.

The crash occurred while President Trump was at Mar‑a‑Lago and had departed on Air Force One earlier that morning, a detail noted in public statements but not directly linked to the accident. The proximity of the crash to the resort has drawn additional public attention to the incident.

As the NTSB proceeds with its inquiry, officials have emphasized that determining the probable cause will require extensive examination of all available evidence. The board’s findings will be released after the completion of the investigative process, providing a comprehensive account of the factors that led to the tragic loss of life.

BBC News reported on the ongoing investigation, highlighting the board’s focus on potential in‑flight breakup, weather influences, and the challenges of wreckage recovery.

articles.title: Fake Alerts Hack Air Raid Apps in Ukraine and Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia reported that their official air‑alert applications were compromised, sending false warnings about nuclear and other attacks, prompting authorities to disable the services and urge users to rely on official channels.
articles.content:
Both Kyiv and Moscow said that their government‑run air‑alert applications were breached on Sunday night, resulting in a wave of false notifications that mentioned nuclear, chemical and street‑fighting threats. The messages were pushed to users of the widely used Ukrainian app and a similar Russian platform, causing confusion and prompting immediate security measures.

In Ukraine, the app normally broadcasts red‑level warnings for missile and drone strikes across the country. On the night of the hack, it also displayed alerts about radiation, chemical attacks and urban combat, reaching residents in the capital and other regions. The false warnings appeared just before a locally negotiated ceasefire in the Kherson frontline was set to expire.

Ukrainian officials quickly responded by advising the public to verify information through other official sources. The air force posted a notice on Telegram stating that the application had likely been subjected to hostile interference, that there was no radiation danger, and that citizens should remain calm while following updates on the service’s official channel. The government subsequently disabled the app temporarily for maintenance, describing it as apparently compromised.

"The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'", said Olena, a resident of Kyiv, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme. She explained that she was accustomed to alerts about blackouts and utility disruptions, but the nuclear warning triggered a distinct alarm. Her husband later received alerts describing street fighting and a separate message written in Russian, which led them to recognize the breach.

The Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee chair, Oleksander Merezhko, told BBC News that the incident did not cause panic, noting that citizens are used to almost continuous alerts and that the use of Russian language immediately raised suspicion. He described the event as an unpleasant but expected part of cyber warfare, adding that the population is largely prepared for such scenarios.

Air‑alert applications are digital tools used by governments to disseminate real‑time warnings about aerial threats, including missile strikes, drone incursions and other emergencies. They typically generate audible alarms and on‑screen messages that guide civilians to seek shelter. Because they reach a broad audience instantly, any manipulation can have significant psychological and safety implications.

Russian authorities reported a similar compromise of one of their alert apps, describing it as a "massive cyberattack" that injected fabricated information into the system. A screenshot of a fake alert, shared by the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh, warned of "nuclear warheads mounted on P1‑Suns" being launched across Russia, used profane language, and urged residents to stock up on food for three weeks and hide.

The Kremlin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, did not comment directly on the breach but reiterated that Russian government internet resources are constantly targeted by cyber operations, noting that the rise of artificial‑intelligence tools is contributing to the frequency of such attacks. Russia’s emergencies ministry later announced that the app’s full functionality would be restored by the end of the day and that the broader alert infrastructure remained unaffected.

Cyber warfare has become a routine element of the conflict between the two nations, with both sides accused of launching attacks against each other's digital infrastructure. Experts suggest that the informal language and profanity used in the hoax alerts point to hacktivist groups rather than official state actors, though the capabilities required for such an intrusion have likely existed for some time. Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday that this may be the first known hack of an official Ukrainian information app, but he expects similar incidents could recur.

The false alerts emerged amid ongoing hostilities that began with Russia’s full‑scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. While fighting continues in various regions, the incident underscores the vulnerability of civilian warning systems to digital manipulation and the importance of cross‑checking information during periods of heightened tension.

Overall, both governments acted swiftly to contain the fallout, temporarily disabling the compromised applications and urging the public to rely on verified channels. The episode highlights the broader challenges of maintaining trustworthy emergency communication in a cyber‑contested environment.

articles.title: Supermarkets in Seven European Nations Disrupted by Suspected Cyber Attack on Refrigeration Systems
articles.summary: A suspected cyber attack forced refrigeration units offline in dozens of supermarkets across Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland, prompting waste of food and financial losses while authorities and retailers work to contain the breach.
articles.content:
BBC News reported that a suspected cyber attack has compromised refrigeration and freezer units in supermarkets across seven European countries, causing temperatures to rise dramatically and leading to significant food waste. The incident was first identified in Belgium and Luxembourg, where around 40 Delhaize stores reported malfunctioning units, and quickly spread to retailers in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

In Belgium and Luxembourg the affected outlets were primarily Delhaize supermarkets, while in Sweden the problem was reported by a branch of ICA in Sjöbo and by seven of the 800 Coop stores. Ireland saw 13 SuperValu supermarkets impacted, the Netherlands reported attacks on at least 17 companies including butcher shops and neighbourhood stores, and Estonia’s Selver supermarket was among those affected. Additional reports indicated that five Spar stores operated by Colruyt Group in Belgium, fifteen Carrefour stores in Belgium and a number of K‑stores in Finland experienced similar refrigeration failures.

Sabcobel, the Belgian manufacturer responsible for many of the compromised units, confirmed that the evaporators in the refrigerators were switched to a defrost mode, causing the internal temperature to climb. The company’s chief executive Stephan Moelans told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber attack and that his team had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network". He added that the simplest mitigation is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection, noting that most customers had adopted that approach after a similar breach in France earlier in the year.

The technical manipulation of the evaporators forced the freezers to heat up to as high as 50C (122F), rendering the stored food unsafe. Local media reported that millions of euros worth of perishable goods were discarded as a result. In the Flemish town of Hoeilaart, a Delhaize branch estimated the loss of produce at €100,000 (£83,500), a figure that did not include additional costs associated with temporary store closures.

Retailers responded with a mix of immediate containment measures and public communications. Carrefour limited the impact to fifteen Belgian stores and swiftly implemented steps to keep all locations operational. Colruyt Group confirmed that five of its Spar outlets had their refrigeration systems attacked. ICA said it was supporting the affected Swedish stores and emphasized that the incident was confined to a specific model of refrigerator. Coop in Sweden stated that the situation was contained and under control, while Kesko’s security experts in Finland began investigations into the cause of the malfunction.

National cyber‑security agencies in Belgium and Sweden announced that they were monitoring the situation, and the United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre said it was cooperating with international partners and industry to fully understand the details of the incident, although no UK supermarkets reported problems.

A cyber attack on connected devices typically involves unauthorized access to the software that controls the equipment, allowing attackers to alter settings or disrupt operations. In the context of supermarket refrigeration, many units are linked to the internet to enable remote diagnostics, firmware updates and performance monitoring. While this connectivity offers efficiency benefits, it also creates potential entry points for malicious actors who can exploit vulnerabilities to issue commands that override normal safety protocols.

Refrigeration systems in commercial settings rely on an evaporator to absorb heat from the interior of the unit. Under normal operation, a defrost cycle periodically warms the evaporator to melt any ice buildup, after which the system returns to cooling mode. By forcing the evaporator into continuous defrost mode, the temperature inside the fridge or freezer rises, compromising stored goods. Restoring proper function often requires physical adjustments to the hardware, as software patches alone may not address the underlying manipulation.

The coordinated nature of the disruptions across multiple countries and retailers suggests a broader targeting of a specific refrigerator model or control platform. Companies involved have indicated that physical modifications to the units are necessary to eliminate the vulnerability, and they are working with security experts to develop longer‑term safeguards. As investigations continue, authorities and industry groups are urging operators to review their network security practices and to consider additional isolation measures for critical equipment to reduce the risk of future incidents.

Matchups include the Vikings against the Lions, the Steelers versus the Browns, and a high‑profile encounter between the Chiefs and the Broncos. The night’s marquee game pits the Eagles against the Commanders on Sunday Night Football, with the Commanders listed as six‑point favorites on their home turf. The Eagles will be without wide receiver DeVonta Smith, who is sidelined with a hamstring issue, and the Broncos will be missing running back RJ Harvey, who is out after a knee injury sustained in practice.

SportsLine’s Projection Model, which runs ten thousand simulations of each NFL contest, has identified the Under 40.5 total points in the Chiefs‑Broncos game as a top pick for BetMGM’s Sunday best‑bet lineup. Entering Week 8 of the 2026 season, the model holds a 58‑51 record on top‑rated picks dating back to 2024, suggesting a modest edge for those who follow its guidance.

Both Kansas City and Denver have struggled to produce dominant offensive numbers this year. The Chiefs rank 14th in scoring with an average of roughly 24 points per game, while the Broncos sit at 25th, scoring just over 20 points per game. Kansas City’s recent performance includes a 20‑3 loss to Seattle, a game in which the team failed to register a touchdown after returning from a bye week. Denver, meanwhile, entered its most recent contest averaging 18 points across three prior games before posting 30 points against a Cardinals defense that ranks at the bottom of the league.

Historical trends for the total points in games involving either team lean toward lower scoring outcomes. The Under has covered five of six Denver games and four of six Kansas City contests this season. In the head‑to‑head series between the two clubs, five of the last seven meetings fell under the projected total, with the only two over outcomes both reaching exactly 41 points. The Projection Model assigns a 55 percent probability to the Under hitting in the upcoming matchup, reinforcing its recommendation for bettors.

If the bet wins, the bettor typically receives the winnings minus the stake, while a loss results in the credit being forfeited. An "under" bet refers to wagering that the combined score of both teams will fall below a predetermined total, a common type of proposition in football betting.

articles.title: Airbnb bans guest cleaning tasks, sparking host and guest backlash
articles.summary: New Airbnb rules prohibit hosts from requiring guests to wash dishes or strip beds, prompting mixed reactions from owners and travelers.
articles.content:
BBC News reported that Airbnb introduced updated house‑rule guidelines that take effect globally from 20 November, limiting hosts to seven standard rules and any other reasonable requests. Under the new policy, hosts may no longer ask guests to perform duties traditionally handled by professional cleaners, such as washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds, or removing rubbish from the property.

One Welsh host, Lisa Clewes, described returning to her holiday let to find the interior in disarray after a group of guests had departed. She recalled broken glasses, cans scattered on the floor, pans left on the table and fish entrails in the garden. "It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," she said. Clewes normally charges a cleaning fee that covers about three‑quarters of a cleaner’s cost and expects guests to empty the fridge, place rubbish in bins and load the dishwasher. The new rules now prevent her from making those requests.

Clewes noted that cleaning her three‑bedroom home typically requires four hours of work. She worries that if guests leave a greater mess, she may need to hire additional cleaners, raising her operating expenses. Those extra costs could eventually be reflected in higher fees for future guests, she explained.

A contrasting experience was shared by Jessica Newhook, who booked a Florida property for an 11‑person family reunion. Despite paying a $250 cleaning fee, the host instructed the group to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, sweep and mop the floors, and even warned that they might be asked to leave if they did not improve their behaviour after chairs blocked the bins. "It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect," Newhook observed, noting that the extensive checklist and rising cleaning charges have diminished the appeal of staying in an Airbnb.

Cleaning‑industry professional Krissi Foskett, who frequently stays in Airbnb homes, recounted a recent stay in Stafford where she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, do a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish to a distant recycling point. While she does not mind helping out, the request made her question the value of the additional cleaning fee. Foskett distinguishes between a considerate guest who places dirty dishes in the dishwasher and a guest who is expected to ready the property for the next arrival. Through her business, she has also encountered extreme cases involving broken furniture, vomit and pet urine, underscoring the challenges hosts face.

Anthony Marsh, co‑owner of a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire, said the new rules prompted him to cut back the number of his listings on Airbnb from five of his twelve properties to just two. He expressed concern that the platform now effectively gives guests permission to leave a “tip” of mess that hosts cannot address. Marsh’s operation does not charge a cleaning fee, yet he noted that industry data shows 63.2% of Airbnb listings include such a fee, with an average cost of £55. He worries that with small cleaning teams and tight turnaround times, additional mess could leave properties unready for subsequent guests.

Laura Lewis, who runs a directory for holiday‑let owners, reported that many of her clients are dissatisfied with the rule change, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect. Some owners are shifting toward direct bookings via their own websites and social media to avoid platform commissions that have risen in recent months. Lewis herself plans to remove the three treehouses on her farm from Airbnb, relying instead on direct reservations.

Not all hosts share the same concerns. Matt Porsz, a full‑time Airbnb manager in south‑west London, believes the update will enhance the guest experience without altering typical behaviour. He asks guests only to lock the property and return the keys, noting that some guests already strip beds or tidy up without prompting, which benefits his cleaners. Porsz trusts Airbnb’s mutual review system to encourage reasonable conduct, stating that a host would not give a five‑star rating to a guest who leaves a property in poor condition. He added that Airbnb is trying to eliminate “silly stuff” that harms the guest experience.

Airbnb is an online marketplace that connects property owners with travelers seeking short‑term accommodation. Hosts may choose to add a cleaning fee, an optional charge intended to cover the cost of professional cleaning after a stay. The platform also features a two‑sided review system, allowing hosts and guests to rate each other, which helps maintain standards and accountability across the community.

The revised house‑rule policy has created a clear divide between hosts who fear increased operational costs and guests who welcome relief from exhaustive checkout checklists. While some owners consider withdrawing from the platform or reducing their listings, others anticipate that the changes will streamline the guest experience without compromising property upkeep. The debate highlights the ongoing tension between maintaining service quality and managing the economics of short‑term rentals.

articles.title: Australia sets record win as Jillaroos crush Wales 124-6 in World Cup
articles.summary: In a one-sided Rugby League World Cup match in Sydney, Australia defeated Wales 124-6, the biggest score and margin in women's international history. Wales' lone try came from Paige Travis.
articles.content:
Australia's women's national rugby league side, the Jillaroos, delivered a historic performance in Sydney, overwhelming Wales by a final score of 124-6. The result established the highest total ever recorded in an international women's match and produced the largest winning margin in the sport's history.

The Australian side crossed the line twenty-one times, with contributions from a range of players. Olivia Kernick opened the scoring, while wing Jaime Chapman added six tries, the most of any individual on the day. Abbi Church recorded two, and other try‑scorers included Jesse Southwell, Jessica Sergis, Kezie Apps, Sariah Paki, Keilee Joseph, Tamika Upton, Keeley Nizza and the goal‑kicker Jesse Southwell, who added twenty points from conversions.

By the interval the scoreboard read sixty points to nil, a half‑time total that eclipsed any previous World Cup fixture, whether in the men's or women's competition. The relentless Australian attack left Wales without a response for the first ninety minutes of play.

The final margin of one hundred eighteen points surpassed the previous record for a women's international match, although the men's record of a one‑hundred‑twenty‑point shutout set by France against Serbia remains untouched. The scale of the victory underscored Australia's intent to secure a fourth consecutive World Cup title.

Wales managed to break the monotony when Paige Travis crossed the line after the Australian tally had reached one hundred points. Her try marked the first score against the Jillaroos in the tournament and provided a brief moment of celebration for the Welsh side.

The Welsh team entered the competition as newcomers, having played their inaugural test match only a few years earlier. This was their sixteenth international fixture and their first encounter with Australia. Earlier in the tournament they had suffered heavy defeats to England and Samoa, indicating the steep learning curve they faced at this level.

Australia struck early, with Kernick scoring in the sixth minute after a well‑executed offload from prop Makenzie Weale. The early try set the tone, and the Jillaroos quickly settled into a high‑tempo rhythm that Wales struggled to match.

Chapman's speed and power were evident as she secured a double on the left flank, while Church powered through on the right. The fifth try arrived when Southwell capitalised on a missed high ball, and the first half saw further contributions from centre Jessica Sergis, second‑rower Kezie Apps and a hat‑trick from Chapman.

Statistical analysis highlighted Australia's dominance: they held the majority of possession in the opening half, completing almost every set of play and maintaining possession for well over ten minutes compared with just a few minutes for Wales. Their efficiency in set completion left the Welsh defence under constant pressure.

The second half continued the onslaught. Within a minute of the restart, Keilee Joseph added to the tally, followed by additional scores from Sergis, Chapman, Joseph again and Church. Southwell's successful conversion of Sergis' fourth try pushed the total into three‑figure territory, aided by a breakaway effort from Tamika Upton.

A Welsh player reflected on the experience, saying, "We just wanted to create a legacy back home for young girls coming through, and I think we did that. The scorelines haven't been in our favour but no one gave up and I am so proud of the girls." The comment underscored the team's determination despite the scale of the defeat.

Rugby league World Cup tournaments bring together national teams from across the globe to compete in a series of matches that determine the world champion. The women's competition runs alongside the men's event, featuring the same rules and scoring system, where a try is the primary method of scoring and is worth four points, followed by a conversion attempt.

The overwhelming victory by the Jillaroos, reported by BBC Sport, highlights the depth of talent within Australia's NRLW ranks and the growing disparity between established programmes and emerging nations. While Wales will look to build on the experience gained, Australia moves forward with confidence toward the final stages of the tournament.

articles.title: Binance freezes half of $6.3bn stolen in record crypto hack
articles.summary: Binance says it has secured roughly $3bn of the $6.3bn taken in a complex hack linked to a North Korean group, while authorities work to trace the remaining funds.
articles.content:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, reported that it has frozen about half of the digital assets taken in what is being described as a record‑size theft. The company said that roughly $3bn of the $6.3bn accessed by the attackers has been secured, while the balance remains in the possession of unidentified hackers.

The breach was initially thought to involve a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, but Binance’s co‑CEO Richard Teng later clarified that the incident was broader. "This was not carried out by one person," Teng said, adding that the hackers employed a self‑destruct mechanism that erased tools and traces, complicating the investigation.

The United States Secret Service confirmed that it is "working around the clock" to identify, freeze, trace and recover the stolen funds. The agency, which leads federal investigations of financial crime, said it will seek to bring the perpetrators to justice. Binance also indicated cooperation with the FBI and noted that its US‑focused platform was not directly affected, though U.S. authorities retain jurisdiction to pursue the case.

Analysts have linked the hack to a North Korean hacking unit, with several firms noting similarities to previous incidents attributed to the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor. Chainalysis expressed "high confidence" that a North Korean actor was involved, while TRM Labs highlighted parallels with the Bybit exchange breach that occurred in 2025. The United Nations has repeatedly identified North Korea as a state that relies on cybercrime to generate revenue in the face of heavy sanctions.

The stolen assets included a range of cryptocurrencies, among them stablecoins such as Tether and Circle, which are pegged to the U.S. dollar. Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value by being backed by reserves or algorithms, allowing traders to move value quickly without exposure to the volatility typical of other crypto assets.

In response to the intrusion, Binance initially halted all deposits and withdrawals. The firm later updated users that deposits remained unaffected while it continued to secure its systems. Binance also announced that it had set aside more than $6.34bn of its own capital to cover the loss and was actively purchasing a variety of crypto tokens to replenish its reserves.

The market reaction was swift. Bitcoin fell about 5% to $76,800 in New York trading on Friday afternoon. Other crypto‑related equities also slipped, with Coinbase down 12% and Robinhood, which offers crypto trading, down 7.8%. The price movements reflected investor anxiety over the scale of the theft and the potential impact on confidence in digital‑asset platforms.

Binance, founded in China in 2017, now serves over 300 million registered users worldwide and reported more than $160bn in assets under custody in 2024. The company has repeatedly assured customers that their funds are safe and that it will cover any losses. However, legal experts caution that such assurances may not be enforceable without contractual backing. Daniel Tunkel of Edwin Coe law firm noted that any recourse would depend on the specific promises made in customer agreements and whether Binance could be sued for non‑performance.

The incident adds to a pattern of high‑profile crypto hacks over the past five years, many of which have been attributed to North Korean actors. While the regime denies involvement, analysts point to cryptocurrency flow analysis and defectors’ testimony as strong evidence of state‑sponsored cyber operations aimed at generating revenue.

Background: Cryptocurrency exchanges act as digital marketplaces where users can buy, sell, and store a variety of tokens. When a breach occurs, attackers typically exploit vulnerabilities in software, employee devices, or authentication processes to move funds to wallets they control. Because blockchain transactions are publicly recorded but pseudonymous, tracing stolen assets often requires sophisticated analytics and cooperation across multiple jurisdictions.

Background: Law‑enforcement agencies worldwide have developed specialized units to follow the trail of illicit crypto flows. These units combine blockchain analysis, traditional financial investigation techniques, and international legal assistance to freeze assets, seize wallets, and pursue criminal charges. The process can be lengthy, especially when the funds are quickly moved through a series of mixers or converted into privacy‑focused tokens.

According to BBC News, the scale of the Binance hack surpasses the $1.5bn Bybit theft of 2025 and represents one of the largest cryptocurrency losses ever recorded. While Binance claims to have secured a substantial portion of the stolen value, the ultimate recovery of the remaining assets will depend on the effectiveness of global investigative efforts and the ability to trace the funds through the complex web of blockchain transactions.

The episode has reignited debate over the resilience of crypto exchanges and the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks. Binance has faced scrutiny from regulators in several jurisdictions, and the current incident may prompt further examinations of its security practices and capital adequacy. As the investigation proceeds, market participants will be watching closely to see whether the frozen assets can be reclaimed and how the broader industry adapts to mitigate future threats.
